chapters.title: Chapter One: The Basement
paragraphs: Burgundy had been awake for thirty-one hours.
He could tell by the count blinking in the corner of his monitor, the timer he set to motivate himself. The number didn't bother him. The shake in his right hand did.

The basement smelled like smoking copper. Three monitors glowed green-on-black in front of him, lines of code scrolling so fast they made the dim room flicker. Cables ran along the floor in bundles thicker than his arm, taped down with whatever he'd had on hand: duct tape, electrical tape, in one place a strip of his own shirt. Against the far wall, beneath a tarp, the prototype waited.
He hadn't looked at it in six hours. That was on purpose. If he looked he'd find something to fix, and he didn't have time to fix anything else. Tomorrow was the day.

Three monitors glowed in front of him: torque curve on the left, strain-gauge table in the middle, and on the right a text editor open on a function he had named GO. On the third line from the top there was an off-by-one error he had been looking at for almost an hour without seeing.

He saw it now. He pressed the tab key. He pressed it again. He pressed it a third time and committed the fix and ran the simulation again and watched the torque curve resolve into something less ugly than it had been.
He let out a breath. An eye twitched.

Above him, somewhere, the palace was quiet. The palace was always quiet at this hour. Even the kitchens, which started before dawn, had not yet started. Burgundy could hear the boiler in the next sublevel, a low irregular cough that had been part of the basement's soundtrack for so long that he no longer heard it unless he listened. He listened for a moment. Then he stopped listening and pressed his hands against his eyes and counted to ten.

He knew the kitchens better than a prince was supposed to. When he was small he had spent more hours there than anywhere in the palace, on a stool near the ovens where it was warm, watching Tuck's mother work.
Tuck's family had cooked for the crown for four generations. People said it the same way every time, *four generations*, as though it were a title, and in a way it was.

Tuck's mother was one of the few people his own mother trusted. She raised Burgundy in between her kitchen shift, and sometimes during, placing him on a stool and tearing the heel off a fresh loaf and pressing it into his hands without a word, still hot enough to hurt, and he would eat it standing up, and the smell of it, yeast and iron and woodsmoke.
He was seventeen now and had been working on this thing for two years. His *prototype, *he called it to himself. This project no one knew about. No one but Tuck.

Two years. Or, that was the official count. The truth was he had been working on something like the prototype for most of a decade, since he was eight years old, when he had taken apart the desk clock in the receiving room and put it back together upside down on purpose to see if his father would notice.

His father had not noticed for two months. When he had noticed, he had cuffed Burgundy on the side of the head and told him to leave the clock alone. Burgundy had taken it apart again that night and put it back the right way, and his father had never mentioned it again.
He thought, sometimes, about the miners. The people the planet ran on.  Their faces, stained black, their dying lungs.  This whole world relied on their arms.

He did not know any of them. He could not have. He was the prince, and the prince did not go into the mines except to stand at the rim during inspections, in the embroidered coat his father made him wear, while the foremen read from their clipboards and the King nodded at whatever they said and the miners below in the pits, black-faced, soaked through, holding their picks at their sides like rifles at parade, looked up at him without expression.

He had been to the rim of the South 12 Shaft three times in his life. It was the "worst" mine. It wasn't just a pit, but a deep labyrinth of tunnels. Burgundy's grandpa's had inspectors who  found some special vein of ore down there. "Never ending" is the how it was talked about. So they just kept digging down. for decades now. It had become infamous for how deep it went. A tangle of tunnels no single person knew the extent of. The elevators to get down to the deepest parts took 30 minutes one way. Or so Burgundy heard from his uncle who used to sneak out as a teenager and explore.

Burgundy only knew the surface of South 12 but remembered the smell. He remembered the way the work lights along the walls made the air look like it was full of something solid. He remembered one miner, a woman working a stretch of rock near the surface, swinging her pick, the working the stubborn rock with a chisel and hammer,  directing the black crumbs that came off that wall into an impossibly old cart. Her sweat seemed permanent.

To his surprise he found himself wondering what she ate. What they all ate while they worked down there.  Probably mushrooms, the pale fungus they called *Greycaps*. It grew along the walls of the deep mines, and his tutor had told him that men cut it and dried it and boiled it into a broth.
On one visit to South 12 the foreman complained that the crews spent their break hours crawling side tunnels searching for greycaps instead of resting.

He thought about that woman sometimes. A lot, actually.  In fact the entire thing he was building in this basement, a makeshift robot with a drill attached,  could trace back to her.  A machine that could replace that woman.

He had not told anyone this. He was aware that it was the sort of thing that would sound stupid if he said it out loud,* I built it for a woman whose name I do not know*, and he was aware that this was also possibly true.
His father did not know about the basement.
Or, Burgundy hoped his father did not know about the basement. It was possible that he did.
His father was the King of Dross, a small planet  taht was mostly uninhabitable ice sheet, but that was packed with valuable ores.

"Our ores make travel between the stars possible" is something his Father would say at the dinner table at least one a month. Whoever sat at the table heard it: Burgundy, a visiting dignitary, a governor, a minister. Burgundy didn't really understand what it meant. He never asked.
The tribute ships came every month and he had watched them for as long as he could stand at a window. Massive cargo vessels descending onto the planet to collect.

From that same window he could see the city. Kettletown. The planet's capital. It fell away from the castle walls in stacked tiers, houses built on the roofs of houses, iron sheeting gone orange with rust.  In the warm months it looked like one great heap of salvage. In the cold months the snow came and settled over all of it and softened the rust to grey.

When he was very small he had asked his father what *tribute *was. What they loaded into the massive vessels. What were they taking away from our planet. *Everything*, his father had said. He didn't explain.

He had learned, eventually, the name of the man whose ships these were. He had never met the man. Nobody on Dross had ever met him. Nicholas was a name his father said the way other people talked about the season's rainfall, as a fact of the world that determined abundance or scarcity. It was all Nicholas.
The basement where he now worked had been a wine cellar once, before some great-great-uncle had decided wine was beneath royal dignity.
The bottles had been carried up and broken in the courtyard to make the point.
He had taken the found the cellar when he was twelve and run the cables down himself, through a vent shaft.

Everything else in here he had scavenged: a motor left to rust in the servants court yard behind the kitchens, ball bearings from a broken serving cart, copper wire he stripped from a wall no one had lit in years.
And then he would work. Not *for *anyone. For himself.
He had told himself, sometimes, that he was preparing for something.
He had not been sure, until tonight, what.
Burgundy finished wiring up the robot's arm. He toggled his controllers to test it out. fluid and smooth. this was working. It would be impressive tomorrow.
"Run it again," he said.

The panel brightened. A line of green resolved on the middle monitor, torque holding flat across the curve where last week it had collapsed. The machine gave the small tone it gave when a routine finished clean, one note, low.

"Good prototype" Burgundy said. He had never named it. Tuck's mom named everything: the boiler and the bread knife, her favorite cutting board, gave them all people-names, and Burgundy had decided years ago that naming objects was a way of lying to yourself. So he just said "prototype" to it.
"He's going to hate it," he said. And sighed a long breath.
The panel pulsed, slow, the way it pulsed when it was only waiting.
He had been careful in his rehearsals not to imagine his father's response.
~~His mother had given him a glance, at dinner earlier.~~
~~That was all. A glance. She had not said anything to him during the meal. She rarely did, when his father was present. ~~

~~But at one point, when the King had been talking to one of his ministers about the southern tariff and Burgundy had been pushing food around his plate, she had looked at him across the table, briefly, and then looked away.~~

~~That night they were joined by the finance minister, The governor of the northern fields, down from the iron country for the season's accounting, the master of the eastern works, who laughed at the King's jokes half a beat before they finished. Two security men whose names Burgundy had never been offered. Three of the men had brought wives, and the wives wore dresses that had crossed systems to reach Dross. They spoke endlessly about things and people Burgundy did not know or have any interest in.  the southern tariff was raised, weighed, and settled in the mild tones men use when the argument has already happened somewhere else. His father spoke last on it, briefly. The minister nodded. The governor nodded. ~~

~~And exactly then, his mother shot him that look again. She was trying to get his attention.  Or was she? He had spent his whole life noticing the things she did not say and trying to assemble them, and he had never quite managed it. Sometimes he thought she watched him the way you watch a clock you have built yourself, waiting to see whether it will keep time. Sometimes he thought she did not watch him at all and he was inventing it.~~
~~He was probably inventing it.~~

The code terminal blipped. The torque simulation had finished and produced an output graph he stared at for almost a minute before he understood what he was looking at. The graph was fine. The graph had been fine the last three times he had run it. He was running the simulation because he could not think of anything else to do, and he could not think of anything else to do because he was very tired.
He looked at his hand. Still shaking
He looked at the timer in the corner of the monitor. The number had ticked over to thirty-two hours.
He should sleep. But he knew he couldn't. His mind wouldn't stop working, not with the pitch waiting for him in the morning.
The boiler coughed below.
Somewhere far above him, the palace clock struck three.
He laid his head down on his arms.

He told himself it was only for a moment. He told himself he just needed his eyes to stop hurting. He told himself a few more things, small reasonable things, and then, between one of those things and the next, he was no longer telling himself anything at all.

chapters.title: chapter 2 The Kings' Hall
paragraphs: The Kings' Hall was the most used room in the castle. It's where all the decisions were made, mostly during morning council.

It was not beautiful. The King had spent his money  elsewhere: a massive boulevard approaching the palace, rebuilt to be twenty lanes wide and flanked with carved stone giants of Burgundy's ancestors; or the stables, rebuilt twice, stocked with beasts from other systems. There was a private hunting ground that had required the forced removal of three villages worth of people, eighteen hundred people in total so that the king could hunt once a year.
The hall did not get any attention.  It was long with arched ceiling, stone ribs fanning out from the tops of the columns, and was mostly empty.  The walls were the same grey stone as the floor.

Down the center of the long hall ran a single pale path, the stone worn a shade lighter by the feet of everyone who had ever  walked from the huge entrance doors to back side of the hall where the throne sat, atop a dais three steps up.

The hall did have one thing worth looking at. Behind the King's throne, a massive window ran nearly floor to ceiling. A thousand small panes of colored glass. And set among them, thin cut sheets of translucent stone, the rare kind pulled from Dross's deepest mines.
In daylight the stone panes would catch the sunlight and split it into gleaming threads of colored light in ways no glass ever could.  And at night the stone glowed faint and pale like embers.

The window was the work of one of Burgundy's great-grandfathers, a king who had been obsessed with the stars. He had taken his cosmology from the Ghai, the ancient underground people who had lived here for a thousand years before Burgundy's clan conquered.
He built the window based on their reading of the sky: every pane placed so that the sun, moving through the seasons, would strike certain stones on certain days.

Each alignment meant something. The light on one stone marked the turning of the year; on another, a planting; on another, the harvest. *What harvest? *Burgundy always thought whenever his tutor would try to explain the cosmology of the big window to him pane by pane. He never asked outloud.
He had asked about Nicholas exactly once, when he was ten, in a geography lesson, in the flat bored voice he had already learned to use for the questions that mattered.
"Where does he keep his fleet," he said, not looking up from the star chart. "Nicholas. Between collections. Where do the ships go."
The tutor did not answer for a moment. When Burgundy looked up the man had gone still in a particular way, his stylus lifted off the slate and held there.
"We do not have that on the chart," the tutor said.
"But someone knows."
"Someone knows," the tutor agreed, and set the stylus down, and pulling out a map of the northern fields as though the northern fields were the most urgent thing in nine systems.
And there was no more talk of Nicholas.
On this particular morning, the one he had been preparing for for years Burgundy had not planned to arrive late.

He had planned to wake at five, with an hour to wash and rehearse the pitch one more time and walk the prototype up the spiral stair without anyone seeing him. He had not planned to wake at seven, sleeve print on his face, the hours-counter showing thirty-five, his neck stiff in a way he could already tell would last all day.

As he rushed to wash his face in the basement basin, he looked over at the robot as it booted up. In the thin morning light it looked smaller than it did at night. It stood on its one fat wheel, chest-high, the salvaged frame bolted and rewelded until the seams showed like scars on its round metal chest and torso with two arms. One for grabbing, and one for drilling rock. The cutting bit at the drill arm's end was ground down to a dull working shine. Low on the front of the robot was a green-glass panel, where his code lived. The brain of the thing positioned where the heart would live. This morning the panel pulsing a slow green pulse, indicating "active", and Burgundy looked at it whole for the first time in six hours and thought, before he could stop himself, that it was either the best thing he had ever made or a toy, and that in a few hours his father would decide which.

The doors of the Kings' Hall were never open during the council hour. He had been walking past them his whole life. He had never walked through them at this hour. But today he did pushing open the great doors and walking in accompanied by a short robot on a single fat wheel that was proving to be quite loud against the stone.

He had not noticed in the basement how loud it was. Down there the ventilation hum had absorbed the sound; up here as he walked the path of worn stone from the door to the throne, the wheel sounded like someone dragging a coin across a slate.

The boy and his robot walked toward the throne. His father sat at the far end, flanked by the long dark council tables filled with rows of advisors and stacked paper. The council was on a break. Advisors talked among themselves, heir voices an echoing hum in the huge hall.
And behind them, the morning light was blaring through the great glass window, splashing colorful light across the floors and walls of the otherwise grey room.
As Burgundy got closer he caught a clear sight of his father on the throne talking to his security minister.
His moment was fast approaching

chapters.title: chapter 3 "I Rule Men"
paragraphs: The King was a large man, broad through the chest, his brow set in a permanent seriousness, his hair going silver at the temples. Around his head he wore a plain band of gold, and set into it, small and unpolished, a strip of each of the eleven minerals the planet gave up.
When Burgundy had been very small he had thought his father was the largest thing in the world. He still thought so sometimes in dreams.

His mother stood beside the throne. Mira's hair was dust-grey, and she wore a gown the color of dried blood. She did not smile when she saw her son. Burgundy felt her watching him .~~ He searched her face for the look she had given him at dinner the night before. He could not find it. She was looking at him a different way now.~~ A tense unchanging expressions.

As he arrived at the foot of the dais, the group started to go silent and look. The advisors stared,  Burgundy snuck a glance of their confused expressions,  the one on the right had a smear of ink on his white collar he did not know was there. The one on the left looked at the prototype briefly and then away.
Burgundy's heart was ramping up.
"Ah yes, Burgundy." Thundered the King's voice into the newly silent room, "You asked to see me,"
"Yes, sir."
"You know this is the council hour"
"I know, sir."
"Then I assume you have something worth the council's time. What is that?" his eye shooting to the robot.

Burgundy stepped forward and so did the Robot, The wheel was loud again. Then it parked and lit up, the panel on its chest pulsed green, ready for the demonstration. It made a soft sound, almost like clearing its throat.
"Father," he said. "I want to show you something."
That was not what he had planned to say.  But the words came out anyway, and the prototype was already glowing, and there was no taking it back, so he kept going.

"It mines," he said. "Or it will, in the fields. Twice as fast as a man with a pick. Maybe more, with proper tuning. I built it from scrap. The components cost less than a month's pay for a single miner. If we built a hundred —"
"Stop."
The King had not raised his voice. He did not need to.
"Father can I —"
"I said stop."
Burgundy stopped.

The hall was very quiet.  The hall was fully silent for the first time since Burgundy had entered it.  The advisors were looking at the floor. Mira was looking at Burgundy. The King was looking at the prototype.
"What do you imagine you have built?" the King asked.
"A miner. A better one."
"And what do you imagine I will do with it?"
"Whatever you want. Make more, put them in the mines. I mean you're the King. You could —"
"I am the King. Yes" His father said it gently, almost patiently, "And do you understand what that means?"
"It means —"
"It means I rule. I rule this planet. A planet whose ores make star travel possible." He smiled a charming smile, and looked around, he was going into a familiar script of his, Burgundy could see it.
"But actually you know what? I don't actually rule this planet. I don't rule Ore. Do you know what I actually Rule?"
Then a pause. Long than was comfortable.
"Men."

He said it softly, the punch line to his well-rehearsed performance. He was smiling broadly now "I rule men. I do not need to mine the mines faster. My job is to rule the men who mine them. Do you understand the difference?"
Burgundy did not answer. His throat was too tight.
The King stood.

He was tall, and he came down the three steps slowly, his robe whispering as they brushed against the stone, and he stopped in front of the robot. He looked at it for a long time. He did not touch it.
Then he looked at his son.

"You think I haven't seen this before," he said. "You think you're the first person to bring a clever invention to our throne? There have been a hundred of you. Every one of them believed he had discovered the thing that would change our world. Make our lives better. Do you know what changes the world, Burgundy?"
"What."

The word came out smaller than he had wanted. He’d anticipated his father asking rhetorical questions and had practiced responses with some level dignity. But here, now, with the wheel silent and the green panel pulsing and his father an arm's length away and Mira's eyes burning into him, the word *what* came out the way it had come out of him at eight years old, holding a clock he had taken apart wrong.
"Willingness" the King said. "Willingness to do what it takes to to keep order and peace. That's what we do here."
His voice was almost kind.

"You are my son. You will rule one day. Ruling isn't just sitting on this throne with this gold band around your head. It's a *craft*. Our craft. It is not learned by playing with robots. It is learned at my side. And you have not been at my side. You have been hiding in the dark, playing with wires, while I have been ruling. What I have given you is the future of this kingdom. And you bring me *this*?"
He kicked the prototype.

It was not a hard kick,  the prototype rocked back on its wheel, squeaking on the polished stone. The green panel flickered, and somewhere along the right side of the hall one of the advisors made a small soft sound that might have been a laugh and might have been a cough.
Burgundy heard it.

In the basement, in the long hours of the night, he had run every scenario he could imagine for how this conversation might go. He had imagined the yes. He had imagined the no.  He had been careful, he remembered now being careful, not to imagine a laugh. He had not been able to bring himself to imagine a laugh.
But the laugh had not come from his father.

The laugh, or the cough, he would never know which, had come from an old man with ink on his collar, an old man whose name Burgundy was not sure he had ever known, an old man who had been standing in this room since before Burgundy was born.
"Take it away," the King said.
"Father —"

"Take it away, Burgundy. Do not bring it back. Do not bring me anything like it again. The next time I see you in this hall I want to see you in council robes. Listening. Learning. Not in overalls. Not with grease on your hands. Do you understand me?"
Burgundy looked down at the prototype.
"Yes, sir," he said.
He did not look at Mira.
He did not look at the advisors.

He turned the prototype around, by hand, because he did not trust himself to give it a command in a voice that would not crack, and he pushed it back toward the doors. The wheel with the loud sound again as it moves across twenty colorful shades of sunlight. The hall behind him silent.  Burgundy walked the length of the hall with his hands on the prototype's housing, and at the doors he did not stop, and he did not look back, and he pushed through into the corridor.
The doors closed behind him.
He stood for a moment with his hand on the prototype, in the long cold corridor where his footsteps would have echoed if he had taken any. He stood very still. Shaking to himself
The prototype hummed beside him. Its green panel pulsed once, gently.

chapters.title: chapter 4 Mira's Wing
paragraphs: Through the closed doors, the council resumed. His father's voice was a low rumble without shape. An advisor answered. Then his father again, longer, and something in it must have been a joke, because it got its soft, polite laughs.
He was still listening when the small side door in the corridor  opened.
His mother slipped out.

She did not look at him. She closed the door behind her without a sound. She stood for a moment with her hand still on the handle, listening to the council, until the King said something else that was answered by the same polite noise, and then she turned to Burgundy, and she put one finger against her lips.
"Come," she whispered. It was less a word than a breath. "Bring it." her eyes dashing to the robot.
Burgundy opened his mouth.
She shook her head, a single small motion, and turned, and began to walk down the corridor.
He put his hand on the prototype's housing. He pressed the small command that told it to follow. The prototype rolled after him.
They walked.

They took a corridor Burgundy knew, the long one that led past the council chamber toward the eastern courtyards. Then Mira turned right, into a smaller corridor that Burgundy had only walked twice in his life. And from here he began to lose his bearings.
She took him past a door he had believed was a broom closet. Behind the door was a narrow flight of stairs going up.
She started up them without hesitation.

Burgundy stopped at the foot of them. The prototype stopped behind him. Its wheel, a single fat wheel, salvaged from a serving cart, rated for stone floors and stone floors only, was going to have to descend stairs.
He had prepared for this, sort of.

Two months ago, in the basement, he had cut the wheel open. He had lined the inner rim with a rubber sleeve. He then wired a small air compressor into the chest cavity. He had coded a 'soft-mode' that would let the tire release air, enough for the wheel to deform around the edges of steps so it could climb them.

It had worked decently this morning as he took the robot up a few small sets of stairs from the basement to the council. But he had never taken it up a full spiral flight. He had not been sure he would ever need to.
He pressed the command.

The prototype's chest made a small hydraulic sound. The wheel visibly relaxed,  it looked, for a moment, as though it had lost some air. Then Burgundy pushed it against the first step. The wheel deformed. It caught. He pushed. The prototype rocked forward, awkward like it was about to fall, but then it mounted the first step, and then the second, and then a rhythm settled into it that was almost a walk. It was climbing.
Mira was five steps up, watching.
"You really built this?" she asked quietly
"Yes."
She nodded once and kept climbing.
Then, three steps up, without turning:
"How long."
"Two years."

The stone at the top of the stairs was a different color, warmer, cream instead of grey, and the sconces along the walls were made of a metal he could not immediately identify, worked with a pattern that looked, when he looked closely, like nothing he had seen anywhere else in the palace. The pattern was intricate and repeating.  The air smelled different too. Not the wet-stone smell of the palace's lower halls. It smelled like books.
Mira did not stop to let him look.

She took him through a small entry hall, and into a larger corridor with a high vaulted ceiling and windows on one side, all shuttered, all dusty. Their shoes made no sound; the floor here was carpeted, a long red runner going grey. Burgundy realized, walking down it, that the runner had not been walked on nearly it all. It felt brand new.
"Mother, where —"
"Not yet."

They passed doors. Most were closed. One was open a crack, and through it Burgundy caught a glimpse of a sitting room, chairs still angled toward each other, but otherwise empty and gathering dust. The whole wing had the feeling of a play that had been rehearsed once and then never performed.
They turned a corner. They turned another.
Mira stopped at a set of double doors, pushed them open, and stepped through into a room that stopped him where he stood.

Burgundy had known there was a library in the palace. There were several. The one near the entrance, where his father sometimes met with foreign envoys, had a wall of leather-bound treaties and a globe that had not been updated in his lifetime. The one off the council chamber held the ledgers and the tax records and the tribute receipts. Neither of them was this.
This library was three stories tall and another two stories down, dug deep into the ground, all contained in this one massive room.

the room was cut up into an intricate labyrinth of bookcases and crossings, stacks running into stacks, with narrow iron walkways bridging the gaps at each level so a person could walk from one wall of books to another without ever touching the floor.  There were ladders on brass rails that traveled the length of each wall.
And doors. Dozens of them, small and arched, set into the shelving in no order Burgundy could find. One was half his height. Another only reachable from the iron walkway above.

A spiral staircase in the center connected the whole thing. Down at the basement level stood the tables. Long, dark, oiled, scattered with reading lamps and stacked books, and on one of them a small model of a star system Burgundy did not recognize. A whole corner had been given over to maps and globes.

It was a striking view. Tens of thousands of books rose around him, more than he could take in at a glance; on the shelf to his left, close enough to read the spines, half of them were in languages he had never been taught.
He stopped. Awed by this huge space he hadn't known about.
The prototype rolled up beside him and stopped too, its wheel humming back to solid mode, its soft-mode air-cycle finishing with a small sigh.
Mira let him look for a moment. Then he asked, "Mother, what is this place?"
She said, without turning:
"This is my library. This whole wing is mine. built at my request when I agreed to marry your father. My mother sent most of these books. This is a piece of my family"
"Your family," Burgundy said.
She turned.
For the first time since the corridor she smiled, a small, thin smile.
"Yes," she said. "My family."

She crossed to a shelf on the eastern wall and climbed the ladder without hurry, and Burgundy followed her up because he did not know what else to do, and the robot waited below on its wheel, its green panel pulsing slowly in the low light. At the top of the ladder Mira walked along the gallery to a specific shelf and stopped in front of it.
The books on the shelf were mostly grey and brown. A few had gold lettering.
One was yellow.
She reached up and put her hand on the yellow book, a plain yellow, no title on the spine, and she looked at Burgundy.
"This," she said, "was your grandfather's."
Then she pulled.

The book came out an inch, then stopped. Something inside the shelf clicked, a small mechanical sound, quiet but precise, and the whole bookcase shifted on some hidden hinge and began to swing inward, silently, like a great door on very old bearings.
Behind the bookcase was another room.

chapters.title: chapter 5 -The White Room
paragraphs: The room behind the bookcase was white.

Actually gleaming white. The walls were paneled in some smooth pale material that was not stone and not wood and not metal exactly. Overhead, no oil lamps, no hanging bulbs, a row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had seen only once before

When he was young, Mira would take him to watch the royal engineers design the planet’s mining machinery. He’d sit for hours if she let him, watching the engineers bent over their drafting tables with rulers and stacks of papers nearly as tall as he was. The engineers worked under rows of long flat panels that shed a bright cold light on their work.

The secret room he was now looking at had that light, that feeling. Even the same smell. The tables were clean. They were laid out with equipment. Not scrap. Not salvage. Real equipment: sealed processors in their original packaging, still bearing manufacturer's marks.; oscilloscopes newer than anything the palace had bought in his lifetime; a small array of green-glass panels stacked between wooden dividers; toolboxes with drawers labeled in a fine hand he recognized, after a moment, as his mother's.

Against the back wall stood a low shelf of documents: folders, ledgers, thin bound reports, all with the same neat spine tags. A stack of manifests. A stack of star charts. A stack of what looked, from where Burgundy stood, like schematics.
She walked to the nearest table and set her hand on it lightly.
"Come in," she said.

He walked to the first table. He picked up a processor. He turned it over. It was a model he had read about in a manual two years old and had never expected to see in his own hand. This one unit was certainly worth more than a year of a miner's pay. There were twelve of them on this table alone.
He set it back down. His hand was shaking again, though not from tiredness this time.
"Mother," he said.
"Yes."
"What is this room? This Library?"

Mira crossed to a chair near one of the tables and sat down. She sat the way she sat at council, straight-backed, hands folded, but her face was different than it was at council. For the first time Burgundy could remember, she looked like a person and not like a queen.
"Your father does not know about this room, and it must stay that way" she said. "That is the first thing to understand."
"All right."
"Nobody in your father's line has ever known about this room and a few other rooms I have in my wing. These are only known to my family"
"Your family?" Burgundy said again, because he still did not understand what she meant when she said it.
She looked at him.
"Sit down," she said.
He sat.
"You know that I was not from here," she said. "You know that your father married me as part of a bargain between families But the version you've been told leaves things out ."
"What does it leave out?"
She considered the question.

"My family," she said, "is not a family in the way your father's family is. There is no title. There is no throne. There is no country. There is only a network. The network is very old and very large and it is spread across nine systems that I know of and possibly more. It moves things. We, move things. Some of those things are legal in some places. Many of them are not legal anywhere. And a large portion of what we move, and what has kept us in business for the last two centuries, is minerals. Specifically the sort of minerals that come from inside this planet, minerals you can't find anywhere else in this part of the galaxy. Minerals that fuel advanced technology like the processors in your hand."
Burgundy looked down at his hand. He had picked the processor up again without meaning to.

"Dross is not important to the Core-world Alliance. We're too far away, too small. But Dross is very important to us. To my family. We move a great deal of what Dross produces. Not through the tribute channels, those are Nicholas's. He takes most. Has for decades. My family picks up the rest. It moves and trades the minerals from this planet, finding whatever buyer will take them, and not asking too many questions about their end use.
She paused.
"Dross has been informally trading with our people for years," she said,  but it was always full of mistrust. Occasional conflicts, because well, my people aren't just traders. They also raid."
"Raid?"
"They find ships carrying cargo in remote parts of the system and raid them. Take them for ransom, or they pillage and sell the cargo"
"So they're pirates?" Burgundy said.

"Yes, you could say that." Burgundy could tell she didn't like the label.  She continued, "Your father's father wanted to formalize trade ties with my family, and my family offered a solution. The solution was a marriage, an alliance built on trade and trust. The marriage was me."
Burgundy could not think of anything to say.
"I was seventeen," Mira said

"I didn't have much of a choice, I was young, and even though I was on a path to study in the Core world academies, your grandfather wanted me for his son. That was the deal. I was the family bargaining chip, every generation has one. I knew I had to be sent here to this place. So I asked for the library. I asked for a whole wing to be built so I could continue my studies.  I wanted it to be big and grand. I had dreams of opening my own academy here. To help modernize this place.  My family agreed to fund the wing. Your father's family agreed to build it.

"For the last 19 years I've been procuring books and technology from the far away systems, using my family's smuggling routes. Every cargo vessel that comes to collect Dross minerals carries a second, hidden manifest, the things I've requested. My cousin runs the family's Dross trade. She has been very helpful."
"What about the academy?"
Mira laughed a resentful gutteral laugh

"Your father would never let it happen. I didn’t know that in the beginning. I was hopeful. Naive, even. But he put a stop to it before it could even begin. He shut it down from the very beginning. Said I could have my books and my wing and my studies but that was to be kept to myself."
Then Silence. Burgundy tried to hold all of it at once and could not.

His mother was a pirate. Not the daughter of some distant royal house, the way he had always been told. Her family ran a cartel, raiders and smugglers who moved black-market cargo across at least nine systems. Though in a way, he thought, that made her royalty after all. Any family that controlled that much trade would command more wealth than most thrones.

And here she stood, the sacrificial bride to secure black market minerals, now surrounded by machines and parts Burgundy hadn't known existed. All of it smuggled onto the planet under her husband's nose.
Burgundy had spent two years believing the basement was the one big secret in the house. But there had been two secrets, and his was the smaller one.
"How does Father not know about any of this?"
"He believes that what I do here is read books. He has not been in this wing since three weeks after our marriage. He has never opened the door to this library. He is not curious."
She said the last word — *curious* — with something like tenderness. It was the first tender thing Burgundy had heard her say all morning.
"Why?" said Burgundy, looking at his mother as if for the first time.
"Why what?"
"Why buy all of this?"

"Because I *am* curious. I always have been, about the galaxy, about the way gadgets and inventions like this can feel like magic. My grandfather lived through the invention of interstellar travel, and when I was a girl he would tell me how it changed everything. Whole systems pulled out of poverty in a generation, because suddenly they could trade with the core world across the stars."
There was a pause. Then Mira said:

"So I have been collecting. and secretly seeding knowledge into this planet. A disc slipped into a servant's basket now and then, carried down to the quarters where someone might read it. A better pump sent to a village that had been hauling water by hand. Small things, quietly, for years." She looked at him. "The people of this planet believe they are poor because the galaxy made them poor. They do not know they have been cut off from it on purpose."
Burgundy did not know how to answer.
"I decided a month ago that I was going to show you this room. Because I've been watching you in the basement"
"You know about the basement?"
"I have known about the basement for more than a year, Burgundy. I've said nothing because I wanted to see how far you would take it on your own."
Burgundy said nothing.
"You brought it to him today" She continued, "your robot. I knew you would. And I guessed the outcome. I told myself that if your father rejects it, it would be time to show you this."
They stood in silence. She walked to one of the tables. and picked up a spool of fine-gauge wire and turned it over in her fingers, once, and set it back down where it had been.
"I am going to offer you a bargain," she said. "Listen carefully. I am going to offer it once."
"All right."

"This room is yours. Everything in it. The parts, the tech. The tools.  Whatever else you need, tell me, and I will get it from anywhere in the system. Even from the Core worlds I can get the most up to date discs and even a fair number of parts.  You will not have to sneak scrap out of the southern shaft anymore.  You will build here, in this room, with real materials. I have already collected discs with some of the most up to date research. And here, you will build whatever you want to build."
She looked at him.
"In exchange," she said, "you will be the prince your father wants."
He looked at her.

"You will show up to council every morning, You will wear the coat. You will listen.  You will visit the mines with your father when he goes, and you will nod when he speaks, and you will smile the way he wants you to smile. You will be seen at the tribute inspections. You will attend the seasonal meeting with regional governors.  You will travel to the docks each month with him to see the tribute shipment goes smoothly. You will be, in every public detail, the son he wanted to have. If he calls on you to speak, you will speak, and you will say what he wants to hear. "
"He'll never believe it," Burgundy said.

"He will," Mira said. "He will believe it because he wants to. That is the thing about your father you have not yet understood. He does not see what is in front of him. He sees what he expects. Give him what he expects, and he will not look further. He will believe that the lecture he gave you after he shut down your robot created a change of heart and that you've grown up, just like he always knew you would."
Burgundy sat with his hands in his lap. He did not look at the processors on the table. He looked at his mother.
"You are asking me to become him," he said.

"I am asking you to look like him. just to keep his eyes away from what you are doing here. if he finds out about this room, it will end very poorly for all of us ***<<<I need to raise the stakes of him finding out. Hint to how bad it would be.***
"Do we have a bargain?"
He thought about it.

He thought about his father kicking the prototype. He thought about the small sound the advisor with ink on his collar had made, the sound that might have been a laugh. He thought about the woman in the South 12 Shaft who had not looked up at him. He thought about the tribute ships coming down each month.
He thought about his father saying *I rule men*.
"Yes," he said. "We have a bargain."

They stood in silence, Burgundy's mind racing as he saw his mother, or some version of his mother, for the first time. And so much started to make sense. the stories she would tell about inventors and gadgets that connected the stars, the errands she would take him to visit the royal engineer. How he would find tools and gadgets on his shelf. In his toy bin. He realized that this moment wasn't random. This was by design. This was his mother's design.
She crossed the room and picked up something from the far table, a small object he could not see clearly until she brought it to him, and she pressed it into his hand.
It was a tiny processor unit. Not the one he had picked up first. A shinier, newer looking one with fine gold lines worked across its surface.
"Begin," she said.

chapters.title: chapter 6 Twilight Freeze
paragraphs: The next day was a rest day, the palace had gone slow and half empty. He went back to his mother's wing in the middle of the morning, but he did not go to the white room behind the bookcase. He walked her library instead, the long deep room, morning light streaming in, illuminating the dust in the massive space. He pulled books down at random and put them back, digesting everything that had happen in the last 24 hours. None of it would sit still in his mind.

He climbed down a brass ladder to the bottom of the library and walked to the long dark table strewn with maps. One in particular caught his eye. It showed the palace in fine ink at the center, and around it and below it, spilling down the steep slope in ten thousand small squares, the city. Kettletown. The capital and the largest city on the planet.

He stood in front of it a long time. Another map showed the whole planet. Mostly white. Only a band across the middle was livable, a third of the world, maybe less: the palace, the mines, the 3 main cities. The rest was ice, and had always been ice. Under the ice, the tutors had taught him, lay more corvite than the whole band would give up in a thousand years, locked beneath ice sheets thicker than the palace was tall. Nobody went out there.
He looked at the streets of Kettletown, the crooked ones that ran down from the wall. He saw one straight street and a label "Bottom Market." And he remembered.

~~His mother was a smuggler. She had told him so the day before without ever using the word. And standing at the map, he remembered: she was not the only one in the family who had snuck things into the palace. He had been doing it for years as well. It was why there was a machine under a tarp in the basement.~~
It had started with Tuck. It always did. They were fifteen.
Tuck was the only person alive who knew Burgundy's face and did not call him prince.
Fifteen was the first time Tuck took Burgundy over the wall, into the city.
It was during The Freeze one year.

For most of a hundred days the sun did not clear the hills. It came up to the lip of them and stopped, a low burning orb. It would give eight or nine hours of a red-orange light that threw no shadows, and then it slid back down the way it had come.
The snow would come in big batches of big  slow flakes. And it would stay, covering the rusted roofs of the city below the palace and turning the whole slope white and soft and quiet.

During the Freeze the palace turned into a glowing temple of light and heat, smoke rising out of a hundred chimneys. The boilers in the sublevels running non stop day and night.  The windows were double thick, and a boy could live an entire Freeze inside it and never once feel the cold on his skin. Burgundy hated this. He hated the way the palace sealed itself. It made him feel cooped up from a very young age.
In the schoolroom his tutors called it the Twilight Freeze,  they gave three weeks off in the middle of it, during the festival season, and that's when Burgundy would sneak out.

They had been born on the same day, Burgundy and Tuck. Tuck's mother told it every year, at both their birthdays, which were one birthday, always held in a little room off the kitchens. A rare mix of servant and royal.

She had gone into labor in the kitchens with a full tray in her hands, the same night the Queen went into labor upstairs. "The two of 'em," she'd say beeming "same night, same cry they both had, the only difference is I still had to get the bread done on time." That was her first punch line

And then, "Beat the queen to it too. Beat her clean. Tuck popped out two hours before Burgundy. Then I had a cry, had a wash, and was back on the line before the noon rush the next day." Everyone would laugh, and now she was on a roll  "Her Highness up there had the whole floor running round like headless hens and I'm down here going, what's all the fuss?" She'd wink at Burgundy when she got to that part.

And Mira would laughed. She would sit on a kitchen stool in that little room with her hands loose in her lap, and she laughed at the Tuck's mom's story in a way Burgundy never heard her laugh anywhere else.

Tuck's great-great-grandmother had been the head cook for the King's great-great-grandfather. They were the rare kind of servant a royal family stops seeing as *just *a servant, and Mira, who trusted almost no one, trusted them.

When Burgundy was small it was Tuck's mother who fed him, who wiped his face, who carried him on her hip through the kitchen steam while his own mother mostly sat behind a closed door in a wing he was not allowed into. The kitchen smelled of yeast and iron and woodsmoke.
Tuck and Burgundy were raised together like brothers. But only to a point.

At six, Burgundy's time came to go to school with the other children of the elite: the security minister's twins, the daughter of the man who governed the western mines, a boy whose father managed the shipping facilites.

They learned figures and the star charts and the history of the clan, while around the same time Tuck went to work. He started in the kitchens the way his mother had, hauling and scrubbing before he was tall enough to reach the counters.

After that, Burgundy saw him in the halls, and that was all. He would come out of the schoolroom in the afternoon and there would be Tuck going the other way with a sack of tubers over his shoulder, his knuckles red from the cold storage.

They would stop. They would talk for a minute, two minutes. Tuck always had something: a rat the size of a cat down in the flour room, a cousin who had lost a finger and kept it in a jar. Then someone would call for one of them, a tutor for Burgundy or *the water is boiling *for Tuck, and they would go their separate ways down the same hall, and Burgundy would carry those two minutes around with him for the rest of the day.
He wanted more of it. He understood, even then, that there was no more of it to be had. One of them wore a coat with the clan's mark stitched at the collar and one of them carried the potatoes.
They found each other again the night Burgundy tried to saw off a wheel.

Burgundy was fifteen and it was the two week break during the Freeze, and had been building in the basement for a year. A mechanical arm that could (almost) pick things up. He wanted to put a wheel on it see if he could make it balance. He had near stripped the palace of every loose motor and bearing he could carry down the vent shaft. But surely he could find a spare wheel somewhere.

He soon found himself crouched in the corridor near the cold storage one evening, slowly sawing a wheel with thick rubber tire off a serving cart without anyone noticing, when Tuck came around the corner carrying crates of eggs. Tuck looked at him mid-saw-on-a-cart's-leg. Burgundy popped up and hid the saw and Tuck's face changed.
"So *you're* the ghost," Tuck said.
"What?"

"Cooks been going on about it for a year. Stuff gone missing. A spring suddenly disappears from the potato scale. The little brass gear out of the coffee grinder, the good one, just gone.  He grinned. "Nothing worth taking. And that's what's got'em spooked, how it just disappears." He looked at Burgundy's saw, "So it's you."
Burgundy said nothing. His pulse was going.

"Relax." Tuck shifted the crates. "I'm not telling no one. Who would I tell?" He said laughing. And that was true. And for a moment and all at once, Burgundy felt something in his chest loosen. Something that had been held tight so long he'd forgotten it could.
It was the oldest feeling he had. Tuck on his side, the two of them against whatever it was that day. That was his everyday, until slowly, then quickly, it wasn't.

So he told him. It was the first time he had told anyone. He secretly building things in that old wine cellar, curretly working on an arm. A motor bolted to a joint that could lift a brick off the bench and set it down again, most of the time. HIs father would be furious if he found out.  And the next version needed parts the palace did not have.
"Oh Ran would have a million of those" Tuck said
"Ran?"
"Ran. My uncle. He's runs a salvage yard in town, I'll take you."
And Burgundy, who had never once been outside the wall, said yes before he had finished thinking about it.

chapters.title: chapter 7 Umberroots
paragraphs: The kitchens took deliveries from the city, and the servants had a gate on the low east side, wide enough for a cart, watched by a man who owed Tuck's mother for a Freeze full of hot meals and found a reason to look at the sky whenever the two of them passed.

The disguise was Tuck's doing: a laborer's coat, brown and worn soft, too big in the shoulder, a cap down to the eyebrows, glasses Burgundy stole from one of his father's reading rooms. ~~and grease worked into the hands, which was no trouble, Burgundy's hands were never clean. The one thing Tuck could not fix was the voice.~~
"Dontchu talk to anyone," Tuck said, the first time and every time after. "You say your words all perfect like you do and you'll give yourself away. Let me talk. You point."
"I will not talk."

"See there you go already *'I will not talk'" *he said in a mocking voice as walked quickly down a servants tunnel that led to the back gate. "Nobody down there has ever said *I will not*. Come on, ghost."

Tuck led the way out the gate, past the guard, and down a path that soon left the palace ground behind and dropped toward the city. The clean stone gave way to packed snow and then to a road of frozen mud.
Ahead, the ground pitched down, and Kettletown came up to meet them, roof below roof below roof, stitched down the whole slope in tin and brick and smoke, the way it had looked from the map.
Houses stood on houses, tin on brick on tin, no plan under any of it, each one leaning on the one below until roofs doubled as the floors of the street above.
Wires ran everywhere, looped wall to wall over the lanes, sagging under caps of snow, spliced and re-spliced at every junction until no one could have said where the power first came from.

Meltwater ran down the wires and froze again into long teeth of ice that Tuck steered him around without looking. Smoke stood up from a thousand stovepipes and went almost nowhere, because in the freeze the air scarecly moved.
A thousand tiny houses with their faint warm light. Pinpricks of orange dotting the landscape of a ten thousand illuminated doorways and windows.
"Welcome to my beautiful city, Ghost" Tuck said, self depricating, half proud. And Burgundy was realizing *Ghost *was becoming his official nickname within their newly rekindled friendship.

They descended flights of uneven concrete stairs serpentining through make shift alleys. And then it came up out of the dusk before he could see the source of it: A smell wafting from somewhere below.

Char, and a spice he had no name for, something dark and warm and faintly sweet that caught in the back of his throat. Then woodsmoke. Then the green raw smell of cut roots. Then a sourness, fermentation, a crock somewhere.
One smell laid over the next, thicker with every step, until they came out of the stacked lanes onto the flat ground at the bottom of the slope and Burgundy saw where it all came from.
"Welcome to the Bottom" Tuck said. "Never thought I'd be taking you here Ghost. This is kinda crazy, keep that coat pulled up around your face."

The Bottom Market ran along a straight road.. The buying and selling took place under a roof of stitched tarp. It was a hundred fires, in a hundred little stalls, and a flurry of dense action that seemed to radiate up off the straight road.

Steam stood up off every fire and stall and hung in the still cold air, a low golden fog lit from beneath by the stove-mouths, and the pale unmoving sun came in sideways under the tarp and turned the steam the color of  honey.
People moved through it close and loud. They were dressed in everything the city had, layered and patched and belted twice against the cold.

They walked past a stall of women cooking around a huge deep pan over coal fire, cutting root vegetables and peppers  and frying them with noodles.  One of the women laughed as she peeled a red potato.

The deeper into the market they went, the denser the crowd. It made Burgundy nervous, being around all these people, but his nerves were overridden with fascination. There was an entire world happening here, a 20 minute walk from the palace, and he had never known about it.
They kept descending deeper into the stream of people and fragrance.
It was the dinner hour. In every stall, stumps for seats and hands wrapped around warm bowls and tins, breath and steam going up together into the golden light.
Tuck was a stall ahead, haggling over something, and for a moment Burgundy stood alone at a pepper seller's table, a woman with a scale and a hundred baskets, and she took him for a customer.
"Go on," she said. "The long red ones. You won't get these up north, not fresh."

He should have pointed. He knew he should have pointed. But she was holding a pepper out to him and asking him a question, and the answer came up out of him in the voice he was born with, before he could stop it, every word of it square and set down in a row.
"Go on," she said. "Taste this one, fresh in this morning, only gunna get worse from here.
He should have pointed. Or walked away.  But she was holding a pepper out to him and asking him to try it, and the answer came up out of him in the voice he was born with,
"Thank you, no. I only wanted to look at them."
It was nothing. It was a polite sentence. Her hand did not stop, but her eyes came up off the scale, the way you look at a coin that rang wrong.

Then Tuck was there, loud, an arm across his shoulders, talking twice as fast and half as clean. "Don' mind him, auntie, he's a bit soft, they dropped him on his head when he was small. C'mon, you." He steered him off hard and did not take the arm away until they were three stalls gone, and the arm was tighter than the grin. "What did I tell you. What did I tell you about the words."

Burgundy did not answer. His heart was going, and the market closed back over the two of them the way water closes, loud and warm and paying them no mind, and after a moment he could breathe in it again.
It was nothing. It was a polite sentence. Her hand did not stop, but her eyes came up off the scale and locked in to him for a short moment.

Then Tuck was there, loud, pulling Burgundy, "Don' mind him, aunt Leel, he's a bit soft, they dropped him on his head when he was small. C'mon, you." He steered him off hard and did not take the arm away until they were three stalls gone, and the arm was tighter than the grin. "What did I tell you. What did I tell you. No talking. This is serious stuff. Don't mess this up."
Burgundy did not answer. His heart was going, but slowly as they walked he went back into taking it all in.
He had always thought the low city would be starving.  he had been wrong.

The stalls were heaped with food he could not account for. Roots, mostly, but roots such as never came to his father's table: a deep bruised purple, almost black, cut open to a violet flesh veined in white; a knuckled yellow tuber the length of his forearm; small round ones, red as coals, sold still clumped with the pale soil they came out of.

And peppers in more variety than he could count. Some hung in ropes from the tarp-poles, dried and fresh both. Some peppers were no bigger than his thumbnail and some long and wrinkled and the color of old blood. He saw one stall cutting a big red fresh pepper, the seeds ripped out, the flesh thrown over an open flame so that the spicy smell of them scorching was half of what hung in the air.

There were pale mounds of the greycaps, the mine fungus he did know. Here they were heaped in baskets in a stall selling 100 type of vegetable. There were greens he did not know a frozen planet could grow.

A woman near him was frying a medly of different colored root strips. She cut them on the bias into thin ovals and dropped the long medallions into a pool of bubbling oil and they went from violet to something deeper as they cooked, the edges lacing black and crisp.

And she turned them with two fingers, the same two fingers she then used to grab a thick pinch of a deep red spice powder that she flicked onto the strips followed by a palm-ful of salt she sprinkled with the same twofingers.
And she was talking the whole time to the man who had ordered them, a long complaint about her son in a slang he almost didn't understand.

She laughed at the end of it, scooping the finished medallions of fried root our with a long perforated spoon, into a twist of waxed paper and dashing  more of a different red powder onto the finished product, this one darker. Then on with a generous dollop of a cool green yogurt flecked with herbs.  She handed it across to the man.

The man took it and dropped two coins on her cutting board, saying something back about her son. She burst out laughing and swatted him away without looking, and the steam went up off the oil into the golden light, and Burgundy stood there in his borrowed coat and could not stop looking.
"Oi. Ghost." Tuck pushed the back of his shoulder. "what are you staring at, man. It's a potato, Come on. you want one?" Tuck didnt wait for an answer.

"We'll take an order of hot umberroots just like that" Tuck said, his eyes following the man as he walked off.  The stall woman nodded and nudged down four potatoes of different shape and color from a hanging basket, and started chopping, "oh and make'em hot" tuck added as he stepped back to rejoin Burgundy who was still taking it all in.
"How," Burgundy said, low, because he could not help it. "How do they grow this? we don't have farms anywhere and there's basically no sun half the year. I thought we shipped in all our food."
Tuck grinned.

"So yes, all *YOUR food *is shipped in, the fancy meat and fruits from other planets. But *our *food" he looked and nodded at the women who was scoring the potato and rubbing it with salt and some tan colored powder,  "it grows down here. And you were wrong. We *do *have farms. They're just not above ground.
"They're in the mines?"
"Yeah, I mean not like *in *the mines where they work, tha'd be crazy and messy but yeah like down there." Tuck nodded faintly at the ground, rubbing his hands to warm up.
"But wait, how? How do they get their energy with no sun?"

"I don't know how it works, Ghost, you nerd," Tuck said laughing.  "Somethin' with the trees. The scrub trees up top, the ugly ones? Their roots go down and the mushroom roots down there come up, and they meet in the middle and they trade."
"They trade?"

"Yeah something like that, the mushroom brings something up, the tree gives it something back. My grandpa used to go on about it when he was teaching me to cook back in the day. Said the mushrooms were like cargo ships." He grinned. "Little ships in the rock, running energy down from the sun to make our farms work. He liked that one, and I did too when I was like *six*"
He paused catching back up to Burgundy's question

"But yeah I don't know it works Ghost, you're the one who went to all that school, I just know they're down there. And they're huge. Like rows and rows of green, most of it hanging from the ceiling of rooms in the rock, mostly old spots they'd mine but that ran dry or somethin'. And yeah, now we farm'em. "  He continued  "Peppers, mostly. That's what we grow. There's like, I don't know, nine hundred kinds of peppers? More? Every color you think of, there's a pepper."

Burgundy was making a connection to one of his father's recurring dinner performances which went something like*You know what nobody understands about Dross?*  *They think it's a  wasteland. Frozen, starving planet, nothing here. They're wrong!  The best food in the system. Easily. Abundance like nowhere else. *
Burgundy had thought it was one of his insecure delusions but now he realized his father was absolutely correct.
The woman was done with their––what was it––*Hot Umberroots * and handed them to Tuck who placed down two coins just as the man had done. Then he gave the paper wrapped bundle to Burgundy.
Steam was racing off the bundle into the frigid air. The medallions of roots were too hot to eat, their oil still dancing on the skin. Burgundy looked around.

The people here ate well and laughed at each other's sons and smiled and his father knew it, and had built a life on top of it in which none of *this* ever came up his hill except the meat, twice a year, and the boast, at dinner, to strangers.
"Eat one Ghost. Quickly before they gets cold." Tuck said.

Making sure his face was still mostly hidden from view, Burgundy bit into one of the black oblong medallions. He had never tasted anything like it. The outside had gone past crisp to almost burnt, and it shattered, and under it the flesh was soft and sweet. Then the spice arrived a beat behind the sweetness, dark and smoky, and then the heat, blooming up the back of his throat until his eyes ran and he had to breathe through his mouth, and it was wonderful. He dipped the second half into the yogurt sauce and ate it. A bright explosion of creamy herby flavor, and some relief to his burning tongue.
And that's when he sensed a flavor that rung familar,

"That heat you're tasting, that's scarr-pepper. That's famous even on other planets because it only grows here, and that one *does* end up in my kitchen, I mean *your* kitchen–– Ha! You know what I mean." he laughed, but it was forced, followed by an awkward silence,
Burgundy did know what he meant. He had eaten scarr-pepper his whole life, in food made by hands he never saw. Or thought about.

Tuck's comment was the first time either of them had acknowledged to each other that it was Tuck who had been making his food all these years, a fact they of course both knew but Burgundy had never consciously thought about. Burgundy looked at Tuck's hand holding the waxed paper of fried roots. A burn scar across two knuckles, old and shining.

Neither of them said anything for a moment. Then Tuck balled up the empty wax paper and tossed it in a fire drum and said, "Come on. Ran's this way, lots more to see" and the moment closed over like it was nothing. Tuck turned and walked back into the sea of people.
They went up through the market slowly, because Burgundy would not go fast. He had never been let alone inside this much real life.
A man sold cups of something they called scald, a hot dark brew thick as broth, ladled from a dented pot half a man's height, into tins you drank and handed back.

A grandmother worked a pot of something red and slow, dropping in the small bold-red potatoes that looked like near perfect spheres, and the smell of it was the spice he had not been able to name from the top of the stair.

Children ran the lanes between the fires with no coats on, screaming after eachother. Nobody stopped them. Everywhere the steam went up and hung and turned to gold in the low light, and everywhere, under the food and the talk, there was something else he noticed only half way through.
It was the machines. They were everywhere, once he saw the first one, and he could not stop seeing them after.

The first one he stopped to stare at was at a stall where a very old man pouring a thin baige batter onto a flat skillet slicked with fat, where it spread and set and blistered, he folded greens and slivered peppers into the fold and pressed it flat with the back of a blade until the edges went crisp, and between orders he cleaned the surface with a ladle of water from a metal jug.
At the foot of his stove, mounted to a metal bar, a fan, taken ouf of an old engine and repurposed here to spin air slowly onto the coals, gently making them glow.

When the man's water ran low he reached back without looking and clicked a small switch, and the fan stopped. Now the motor was turning a small pump mounted to the other side of the same bar, the pump pulling meltwater up a hose into his metal jug. He looked away, bored as he let it fill. Then he clicked the switch back and the pump stopped and the fan started up again, feeding the fire. One motor that did one thing or the other, never both.

"You've got'em on the one motor," Burgundy said. He had not meant to say it out loud. But he did try to adopt the slang. He kept going, "Both of them, off the one. So you can only ever run the one at a time. The fire, or the water."

The old man did not look up from his skillet. He flipped the folded batter, pressed it, let the edge crisp. "Can't blow on a fire with no one to feed." Burdungy wasnt sure what he meant, and he moved on, luckily Tuck hadnt seen the interaction.

Further on, a mom had run a length of copper gutter down off a warm roof, where the meltwater came steady, and set a wheel under the fall of it. The wheel was an old mine drill rotor with small tin cups riveted around the rim, and the water dropped into the cups and turned it. Fast. And the axle ran back through a train of mismatched gears into a coil of wire wound on a nail-studded spool. A single bulb hung off the end of the whole thing, burning steady the woman as she fed her newborn off her chest.
"You're doing it again," Tuck said. "That thing with your face, which by the way you need to cover better"
"What thing."
"Like every busted fan and light bulb is a miracle." He steered him on by the sleeve. "It's a fan, Ghost. It blows on a fire. My nan had one. Everyone's nan had one."

But Burgundy could not stop. Up the hill, in the palace, a fan that broke got carried off by a man whose whole job was carrying off broken things, and a new one came from a crate, and no one ever saw where the crate came from or where the broken one went.
Down here nothing went anywhere. It got opened up and stared at and made into the next thing.
"Everyone's nan had one?" Burgundy said. "Nobody in the palace could build anything like this."
"Course they couldn't." Tuck said it like it was obvious, and to him it was. "They don't have to."

They passed a woman feeding peppers into a mill rigged to an old sewing table. She was controlling the grind with a rocking pedle she was pumping with one foot under the table, the drive belt that was patched in two places with wire and so it did not quite run true, and the whole rig ticked once each turn.
She kept the rhythm without looking, both hands feeding dried peppers into the grinder's hopper, red dust coming out the bottom into a metal bucket and wafting into the street.

But the one that held him longest was near the top of the stair, where the stalls began to thin. A boy no older than Burgundy sat framed by a thin doorway, behind a machine no bigger than a loaf of bread on a small wooden table. Beside it sat a basket of copper wire, salvaged, a rat's nest of kinked and tangled wire, the ends gone green. His little contraption was feeding in wire from the tangle on one side and channeling it out the other, winding it tightly around a spool in tight even rows.

The boy was not watching it. He was eating a strip of fried red potato, one-handed, watching the lane, while turning the crank the drove the machine's delicate movement through a series of mismatched gears.
Burgundy had been winding coils by hand in the basement for four months. His were lumpy and uneven, and he wound and unwound and rewound them, and he hated every hour of it.
He stood in front of the boy's machine and did not say anything. His eyes feasted on the build.
"You need something?" the boy said, not friendly, one hand holding a fried root drenched in sauce.
"Relax, Thresher, he's not buying." Tuck was already pulling Burgundy off by the sleeve. "He just likes staring at junk. Don't let it go to your head."
The boy looked at Burgundy a second longer, decided he was harmless, and went back to the lane.
"Ok we're done staring at things" Tuck said, a note of increased vigilance in his voice.
"We gotta get to Ran's and then get back."
They came to the end of the stalls. The market noise fell away behind them and then. A big empty square.
At the head of the square stood a tall ornate building, made of warm stone with a row of tall doors, the Custom House, where the crown ran the operation that weighed and shipped the Ore.

And in the middle, stood a statue three times the height of a man: Burgundy's grandfather, a decade dead, cast in dark metal, one hand out over the empty square, a minecart by his side with markings Burgundy knew was the language of the Ghai

Near the foot of the statue a ring was painted on the stone White once, flaking now, wide as a house. Inside stood two tall grey soldiers, masked helmets, standing still, the only other people in the square.

"Nicholas's men," Tuck said, low, as they walked along the edge of the square. The ease had gone out of his voice. "It's collection day tomorrow. They always send a few of their men here a day early to just, I dunno. They're helmets never come off, they just stand there in their little rings, all night, all day, until the big  ships come to collect–– the stuff."
*The Stuff*. Tuck didn't know the word 'tribute.' nor all it meant.

"And we're not allowed to cross into that circle." He said, "No, no. Bad news if you do. My neighbors uncle went into one once. Drunk, years back, to be funny or somethin'. Put his hand on a soldier and kissed its mask. And it ended poorly for him"

Tuck sped up their walking and his eyes tracked the soldiers. "His whole family had their stipend cut for 20 days, and the guy–– the uncle, was gone by morning. Not killed that anyone saw. Just, gone."

He shrugged,  "My mom says Nicolas is the reason no one invades Dross and to just be grateful and not mess with them. But if I ever meet the guy I'm gunna tell him to chill out with these soldiers. They're not just here, there's a bunch all over the city
They left the square, and after two more turns they were standing in front of a house made of scrap. Walls made of tin sheets and old doors and a section of ship's hull, all lapped over each other.

A yard opened off the side of it behind a fence of stacked drums, and the yard was full. Heaped really.  Seemingly sorted, but into hills: a hill of motors, a hill of rats nest wire, a hill of pipe furred white with frost.
Smoke came up thin from a pipe in the roof. And someone moved inside.
"Ran's!" Tuck said.

chapters.title: chapter 8 Ran's
paragraphs: "Tuckey my guy!" Ran belted when he opened the door to them. "How you doing partner? Your mom send you with anything special for me?" Ran asked.

Tuck pulled from his bag a purple fruit like the ones Burgundy would occasionally see sliced at breakfast, and passed it to Ran. "Nice!" He eyed it, "Another one of these fancy fruits you all eat up there. Beautiful. Oh come in." and then he took a bite and turned "And who's this?" he said through a mouthful of the purple fruit.
"A friend. Back on leave from the North fields." Burgundy nodded, Ran looked at him once but was diverted by Tuck who was already pushing into Ran's house scanning the shelves.
Ran was Tuck's uncle, his mother's brother. Thirty-something,  years old, with a beard and kind eyes and scars on the tops of his forearms seemingly burns,
The house was equally as packed as the yard, though where the yard was heaps, the house was order. Every wall was shelves, floor to ceiling, and every shelf was jars, hundreds of them of all sizes.

A jar of springs, a jar of small brass gears, a jar of switches, 20 jars alone dedicated to screws. What would not fit in a jar hung from the beams: coils and lengths of chain, hooks and tools whose use Burgundy could not guess.
A fire burned in an iron stove in the corner. On top of it a pot ticked and steamed, something with that same pepper the grandma was braising in the market.
An old white dog had come in from the doorway and lay against the warm iron, legs fully extended.
Burgundy knew what he wanted for his metal arm project. But in here his mind began to expand to all the many other things he could build with the stuff in this room.
Tuck did the talking and Burgundy pointed: a set of bearings, a spool of the fine copper, a small gear train still packed in the grease of whatever it had come out of.

Ran named a number and Tuck laughed at it, and Ran named it again, slower, and they went back and forth in a fast half-serious-half-banter rhythm of numbers Burgundy could not have joined if his life depended on it.

Ran stepped up a stool and reached the top shelf, bringing down a squat corroded metal canister, fist-sized, casing gone green and crusted. He set it on the counter like it was worth something. "Now this," he said. "This I don't give away. It's a governor core. Off a cage lift, the kind that runs the ore up the deep shafts to lift the shipments up. More power than 50 motors when it was new.
"Yeah but its not new, it's a dead corpse uncle, what are you even asking for it?" said tuck as he lifted the unit to eye it
Ran told him.
"Are you—" Tuck put it down like it had bitten him. "Are you joking? For that? You're insane. You've actually lost it out here in the cold."
They started arguing and then,
"It's worth more than that," Burgundy blurted out, the first thing he had said since entering the house.
Tuck stopped mid-word. Ran turned his head.

Burgundy could not stop himself. "It's a graded core in there. The casing's dead, that's just tin, it's meant to rot. But the core inside is osmarine. Probably low grade. But still Osmarine. It has negative mass, makes things float. You crack it careful and sell it right, it's worth ten times more than what you just asked." He nodded at it, stiffly, and then a pause "You're underselling it." He said as if their silence was because they didn't understand his point.
Nobody said anything.

Ran looked at him, really looked, the small eyes going still, and Burgundy understood that a boy from the north fields did not know the words *graded core*, and that his hands, grease and all, had never held a pick, and that his face, despite the stolen glasses, was on the coin in Ran's own pocket.
Ran looked at him for a long time. Then he looked at Tuck and said, slowly, "low grade osmarine. Right."
"Well I think we have all we need for now" Tuck said in a cheery voice, that covered the moment well.
Ran wrapped the parts in oiled cloth, tied the bundle, pushed it across, and took the coins Burgundy had counted onto the table.
Burgundy took the watermelon sized bundle from Ran who held the other end a moment longer than he needed to before letting go, his eyes fixed on Burgundy.
"Whatever you're building," Ran said, to the bundle and not to Burgundy's face, "make it worth what it costs." He let the bundle go. "Everything down here costs somebody something."
For the second time, someone had said something to him whose meaning did not fully land.
He walked them to the door, the sleeping white dog, waking and following like it was his reluctant duty to walk them out.
At the edge of the yard Burgundy glanced back and saw Ran watching him go, and knew he had not been fooled, and that Ran had decided not to ask. Not to know.
They climbed back through the freeze as the sun was finishing its feeble rise for the day, the sky turning a grey blue, and large flakes of slow snow wandered their way to the ground.

The two boys passed the bundle of parts between them when their arms got cold, and Tuck talked the whole way, low at first and then back to his big self, going on about a cook who had wept over a sauce he botched, and about the critter who snuck into the cold storage and they found it frozen solid, and Burgundy laughed twice, out loud, which he never did inside the walls, because inside the walls there was no one to laugh with.

Halfway up Tuck stopped to breathe and looked back down at all of it, the stacked and lit-up dark, the gold fog of the market floor, a vein of orange among the blue, and ten thousand stovepipes going up into the cobalt sky.
