"Best place on the planet," Tuck said, "and they built the palace so you'd never get to even look at it." He grinned. "Idiots."
Burgundy looked at it too, breathing hard from the climb. He had come down here thinking the machine in the basement was his, a thing he had made because he was made different. Special.

But then he had watched a man run a pump and a fire off one motor. He had watched a boy his own age wind a perfect coil with a mill crank. Nobody on that slope lacked the mind to build what he built. They lacked the parts. Parts, and the time to waste.
And in that moment he so deeply wanted to give them all of it. He did not know yet what that meant, and he did not chase it. He just carried it up the hill with him with his bundle of parts.

chapters.title: chapter 9 Nicholas
paragraphs: That was the boy he had been.
They snuck out five more times that year, and the sixth time the security minister's people were waiting at the low gate.
Soon he was in the office of his furious father

*He was sixteen*, he seethed. *Nearly a man*, and there would be *no more of the cook's boy. Kings did not keep friends in the kitchens*. It was time he learned the difference between the people he ruled and the people he kept.
So that was the end of it. Not a falling out. He and Tuck were just pulled back to opposite ends of the same hall, by the same force that did it the first time.
Tuck was in the kitchens still. They passed sometimes, two minutes at a time, and neither of them ever talked about their little flash of adventure and friendship when they were fifteen.

And now he was seventeen years old, and sitting at a long dark oiled table in his mother's secret library, wondering what he would do in the white room behind the yellow book. And how he would make good on the other side of the bargain, the promise to become the *Prince your father expects you to be.*

From that day on he lived two lives. Protocol ruled one. Sunlight streaming through a thousand panes of glass and stone. An embroidered coat, as he performed his expected role. The other took place after dusk, behind a nondescript yellow book high up on a shelf.

Burgundy threw himself into being the perfect prince, but the work took a toll. He felt it grind him down. A dull ache behind his eyes always after a day of it. It was the quiet hours working in the secret bright white room, surrounded by possibilities, that renewed him.
The months went on and neither life knew about the other, and Burgundy carried an increasing fear that his father was on to him.

But the more time passed, the more he realized Mira was right. His father seemed to believe nothing was amiss. That the lecture had worked. The days he spent in the light of the colorful window, by his father's side, he realized that the King saw the son he expected to see, the boy finally bent into shape, and he did not look further.
He had a growing curiosity about Nicholas, The tribute. The arrangement the planet was in. How did it work?

He stayed late one after council. The council chamber emptied slowly, Burgundy waited until it was nearly clear and then went to the steward at the side door, an older man he had seen every day of his life and could not have named.
"The old ledgers," Burgundy said. "The tribute accounts. Where are they kept."
"With the master of records, sir."
"And where is he."
"I could not say, sir." The steward looked at a point just past Burgundy's shoulder, the way they all did. "Shall I send word that the prince asked?"
Which meant his father would hear of it by evening. Burgundy heard the protective trap in the courtesy and stepped back from it.
"No," he said. "It's nothing. I was just curious."

"Very good, sir," the steward said, and held the door, and did not watch him go, and Burgundy went out into the corridor thinking that his mother had used that same word, curious, and made it sound like the most dangerous thing a person could be.
With time he was surprised now much he learned just sitting in council for hours a day listening. And after a few months he started to get the full picture on the Tribute.
Nicholas provided security. That was the word the ministers used, *security*, always without irony, and it took Burgundy three months of listening to understand everything the word contained.

Dross sat in a remote, dangerous part of a remote system, months of hard travel from the lanes of the Core World Alliance. The Alliance's markets were distant; its protection was theoretical. A planet full of minerals with no fleet of its own was like a warehouse of valuables with the doors unlocked. Nicholas kept the doors locked.

No one on Dross had ever met Nicholas. Not the King. Not the King's father, or his father. Four generations of the royal line had ruled this planet fearing Nicholas's name and not one of them had heard his voice or seen his face or received so much as a single word.
Nicholas's ships patrolled the approaches. But Nicholas's name, more than his ships, kept the raiders of six systems from descending onto Dross to pillage or conquer.

In exchange, Nicholas took unrefined ore. Around 70% of what they produced. The royalty of Dross had resented the bargain for four generations and yet for four generations they had complied, because it worked, and because nothing else would.
Every resource-rich planet in the region lived under some version of this arrangement. It was not an alliance. It was extortion with a schedule. The ministers did not call it that.
Burgundy learned to come early to council

The ministers gathered before the King arrived, in the grey hour, before the sun illuminated the big window's panes. They warmed up over stimulating root tea, bitter and faintly numbing. Sweet bread, torn and passed. Loose talk, before they put their public faces on.
He said little.
This morning they were discussing  collection, which was five days out, the tally sheet spread down the main table. Burgundy set down his cup. "What happens if we come up short?"
The table looked at him. It was the first meaningful question he'd ever asked to these people.
The oldest man in the room answers. Vharush was the minister of mining. He a face like a TK,  one eye gone milk-pale from a rockburst forty years down.

He glanced once at the closed doors before he spoke. "It's happened. only once in recent memory, before your time. Eastern works, a governor came up short on corvite one month, and didn't know it." He tore his bread. took a sip of tea "Bad count. Books said he was fine. Eight percent short and nobody caught it."
"So what happened?" Burgundy said.

"The ship came, took the load, left, same as any month. Three days on, another ship came back. Didn't collect. Came down over the governor's own house, hundred meters up, and stopped." Vharush turned the bread in his fingers. "Eleven days. this huge ship, big as a district, hanging over his roof, throwing his compound into shadow half of every day. Took nothing. Dropped nothing. Sent no word. Just hung there."
The room had gone quiet.
"By then they'd torn the books and weight logs apart and found the eight percent discrepancy and had to get to work.

Whole shafts on round-the-clock shifts. By the twelfth day the governor had the missing stuff and shipped it to the capital, flew along side the rigs as they drove to deliver it himself. The ships followed,  Ship took it that night off the cargo field and was gone by morning. Never a word, start to finish."

"There," the trade minister said, reaching for the tallies. "That is why the count has to be right the first time. That is why the sharpest men on Dross sit in the Custom House and nowhere else. We do not miss eight percent."
Burgundy was confused about something, "But how did he know it was that one governor who had fallen short. Aren't all the minerals pooled together for the collection"

"That's the part I never followed." said a young minister who had been looking at his cup, rotating it in his hand.  Every district pools into the one house before it ships.  There's no line in any book that says which region came up short. So how did Nicholas know whose house to sit over?"
A pause. One or two of them frowned at the question, thinking
"Bad count's a bad count," Vharush said, and reached for the bread. "Point is you don't hand him one."

Burgundy's mouth was. numb, his mind sharpening as the tea took effect. And in the silence and followed the story, he was taking in another lesson, not one about book keeping. The young minister had asked the only question that mattered, *how did he know,* and Vharush had answered with a proverb about accounting.

These were the smartest men on the planet. ANd every ounce of their effort went into one thing: *get the number right, get it delivered, do not come up short. *That was the whole of their genius now. Not *why* they paid, or *whether* they could stop, or *what* it meant that a faceless man could find one guilty roof in a hundred districts. Those questions had been trained out of them, or out of their fathers.
The sun peered over the horizon and shot light through the vast window, shooting a million threads of lights into the vast hall. The King entered through the double doors, walking briskly.
"Good morning Gentlemen." he said in the cheer he wore in the last days before a collection. "Let's get to finalizing the tally."

chapters.title: chapter 10 The Claw
paragraphs: The nights belonged to the white room.
He found his own ways up. That was the first project. His mother's route through the broom-closet stair was hers; using it risked pattern, and pattern risked notice.

The palace's roots were deeper than its towers. Old dungeon galleries, drainage vaults, dead corridors sealed and forgotten by men who had died before his grandfather was born. And through his exploration he discovered that Mira's wing had been built onto a disused arm of one of these subterranean complexes, its foundations grafted into the old cells.
Over the first month he mapped three separate routes to his mother's wing, each surfacing through a different forgotten door.
In the white room, for the first few months, he read. And only read.
"I had someone leave your boxes in the room," His mother had muttered to him discreetly at breakfast in the first month. "They're all discs, as you requested."
He wondered what *someone *she trusted with her secret, but didn't think too long about it. He was thinking about the discs.  The discs, he came to understand, gave shape to the whole civilization.

There was no live connection between the stars. That was the fact underneath everything, the fact the Core World Alliance's own maps politely minimized: information could be beamed between systems, but a signal took months to cross what a ship crossed in weeks, the signal decayed and stuttering by the time it arrived.

So knowledge moved the way freight moved: in batches, on hulls. The great relay stations of the Core worlds gathered transmissions the way harbors gather cargo, wrote them onto discs, and the discs rode out along the trade lanes toward the periphery.

A disc was a slab of pressed crystal the size of Burgundy's palm, dense with more text than the palace's three libraries combined, and by the time one reached Dross the research on it was a year old at minimum, often three. It did not matter. On Dross, three years behind the core was still fifty years ahead of anything else on the planet.
Mira's cousin, Ressa, brought the discs in with the cargo runs. They would come in a small wooden box with divider slits, packed with wool and sawdust.

In those first few months, Burgundy didn't build a thing. All he craved was more discs.  He would slip his mother a written list, folded into the book she was reading at breakfast, and two or three weeks later a crate would arrive in the white room, labeled in the formal Core-world dialect he had learned from his tutor but now had to teach himself to fluency.

He could slip a disc into his terminal and start reading: journals of the core-world academies, engineering symposium collections, survey papers that mapped whole fields in a single sitting, patent filings by the hundreds, each one a blueprint of somebody's solved problem.

One night, working late through a journal 14 months stale, he read a short paper on how a machine in a lab could be taught to close its claw hand around an object: not by measuring the object first and computing a grip, but by squeezing, slowly, while a gauge in each finger reported the strain, and stopping the instant the numbers said the hold was firm.
He read it twice. The machine could teach itself. Improve itself based on feedback from its own action.

He looked over at the corner, at the pile of old projects he had carried up from the old wine cellar basement. Among the pule was the claw. The one he had built at fifteen out of Ran's parts, three jointed fingers that could lift a brick. He hauled it out, bolted it to the bench, ran a cable to his terminal. He set a clay cup in front of it, and keyed the instructions for the claw to bend and grab.
It sprung to life, bending over. The fingers closed around the clay cut. It shattered.
Too hard, too fast. The problem, he came to understand, was that the arm was half blind. One coarse gauge per finger, reporting late.

So over the next three weeks he rebuilt the claws hardware from the fingertips in. Fine strain gauges laid into each finger, reading many times a second instead of once.  Pads on the fingertips that could tell holding from slipping, so a cup easing through the grip read differently than a cup resting in it.
And under all of it, the code loop from the paper: squeeze by the smallest step, read everything, stop at firm, and log the number. Every grip taught the next grip. Every failure was a lesson filed.
Clay cups kept coming down from the kitchens under his coat, and kept breaking. He swept the shards into a crate.
Then one night, thirty broken cups in, the claw came down, closed, and stopped, and lifted. The cup stood trapped by the finger as it lifted up.

It was the first time the hand had chosen. He had not told it the cup was fragile. In the half-second of closing it had felt the cup push back and decided, on its own, not to break it, and it would remember the number forever. He sat with it a long while, lifting the cup out of the fingers and setting it back, watching the grip come in a little truer every pass, and somewhere in that hour the last of his patience for only reading burned off.
It was time to build.

He began reading to build and building to know what to read next. Every few weeks a stack of boxes came up from the cargo field. Crystal discs packed in wool and sawdust, and crates with . a dozen more of somebody's solved problems pressed into crystal, and he carried them down through the dark and fed them into the machine one paper at a timeAnd inside were parts unlike anything Burgundy had ever laid eyes on.
Tin-fulls of ball bearings that turned with a breath, a motor still in its foam, shiney sharp drill heads. Bright spools of never-used wire.

One box he forgot he ordered. He opened it to pull out a He opened it to pull out a leather apron, cut heavy and supple, oiled to a shine.  He had ordered it months ago from one of the catalogues his mother left him. This would be his uniform at night.

Building with these parts and tools felt easy compared building with scrap. This was more like putting together a puzzle. So his arm improved faster  than anything he had ever made. Within a month it could hold anything he set in front of it, an egg, a wrench, each at its own true pressure.
He gave it more fingers and a palm and soon it looked more like a human hand. Soon it could pick up and hold a handful of gravel.
Holding was no longer the interesting problem. It sat there on the bench, this clever patient hand, and it had nowhere to go.
He looked across the room at the crates he bought to replace the one fat serving cart wheel from his last prototype.
Tracks: Thick rubber belts cleated in steel, the kind that ran the big rigs down the deep mines, three matched pairs.
Het unpacked them and lined up a pair and stepped back. And in that moment, it all began to clarify in his mind.

He put the terminal to sleep and pulled a fresh sketchpad Core world sketch pad of thick paper the color of cream. And an unopened tin of pencils, wood of a dark oiled grain, a tip of some black mineral he had never seen or heard of, but that glided like ice across the page.
And he drew.

Not the arm. The whole thing. A body to carry, low and armored, two arms loaded with a suit of tools.  Lenses for eyes, so it could see the rock instead of being told about it. All running on the treaded tracks so it could take gravel and slope and rubble and stairs.

Draft after draft he saw that this was no longer  a drill bolted to a frame on a wheel. It would be a robust mining robot whose brain would be an array of processors a million times more powerful than the brain that powered the robot his father kicked.

The pencil moved all night to keep up his blossoming visions, and he had a feeling he had not felt since he was fifteen on the far side of the wall with Tuck, which was the feeling of being about to build something that had never existed before.

chapters.title: chapter 11 The Custom House
paragraphs: By day he continued to be the prince his father expected. The King had begun to teach him in earnest. To take him to meetings.

Any hour he had his son beside him and a quiet minute to fill, he filled it with the *craft*. How to tell if a governor is lying or gossip on every advisor at council disguised as *this is stuff you gotta know *and *the parts of ruling he said no one would teach you honestly*.

Which was how Burgundy came to find himself in the center of Kettletown one warm morning.  He was steps behind the king, flanked by lines of soldiers, walking across the central square toward the Custom House at the head of it.
He had been here once, on a cold evening the first time he and Tuck had snuck out.
They walked past the flaking white circle where Nicholas' men stand during the tribute collection.

They walked past the statue of Burgundy's giant metal grandfather raising one hand by a minecart. In the daylight he could see that the Freeze had streaked it with rust, so that the old king appeared to be lifting a hand that had begun to bleed.
The trade minister was waiting inside the Custom House when they entered. A narrow man with ink worked so deep into the creases of his knuckles it would not wash out.
"King Vorran, it is our pleasure to have you here today"
"Thanks Gitz," as they walked up the stairs and toward the ministers meeting room,  "now lets get right to work on the price assessment"
The meeting room had a long table with ledgers sprawled out on the table in a way another man might lay out a feast.
Along the wall stood a row of glass jars half the height of the king , lit warm from within by lamps set into their bases, so the whole row glowed like a line of standing lanterns in the grey room.

And inside each one, hundreds of small marbles of mineral. A cylinder for every mineral they mined on dross with a label and a scientific marking symbol. Every mineral the planet gave up, rendered into little spheres.
"How many?" Burgundy asked the minister as they walked past the mineral sample "How many minerals do we mine?"

"Eleven," the minister said, pleased to be asked  "Eleven that are actually useful." he pointed to a map on the wall of the whole country, color coded by what minerals were found where and at what depth. He started pointing

"Iron in bulk out of the north, where the seams run shallow and wide. Easy. A group of kids could dig the north." He chuckled and continued, "Copper and tin from the eastern hills. The rest are our specialty ores. they mostly come up out of the deep shafts in the south, near the palace. They're the ones that take men." He said casually as he tapped the dark blue shading that indicated the southern mines.
Gitz walked him down the row of jarred marbles the way a proud man walks you through his collection of wine.
"Corvite" he said pointing to a jar blue-black marbles "Every terminal and processor in the galaxy runs on a core made of this"
He moved to another jar
"Threnite. Holds a charge and never wears. The powercells in ships need a lot of this stuff"
"Greyiron the workhorse metal, basically every building in the core words is built with this."

"Voltrine, which is abundant and basically  worthless unless you refine it down past ninety-nine parts pure, and then one thimble of it runs a reactor for a year. refine it more and it goes into weapons."

Then he came to the last jar. It was smaller than the others. A single cylinder, and inside it, not resting on the bottom but hanging in the middle of the glass, one ivory colored marble, much smaller than the others.  turning very slowly on nothing.
Gitz went quiet in front of it.

"You'll have had this in school," he said, "but you'll not have stood next to it." He put one ink-stained finger against the glass, near the little floating orb, and did not tap it. "Antibarytic osmarine" The marble turned and the minsiters voice went even quieter, more profound,  "This is the reason we can travel between the stars. It is not like other matter. Other matter has weight, Osmarine has the opposite of weight"   ~~Set enough of it in the right place and the space around it forgets how far apart two points are supposed to be." He watched the marble~~.
Burgundy looked at the one pale sphere hanging in the lit glass.

"Eighty-three years since they learned to mine it and refine it," Gitz said, and for the first time all morning he did not sound like a man giving a practiced lecture on minerals. "Before that, the stars were closed. You couldn't hold a door open in space long enough to cross the galaxy. Osmarine is what holds them open. "
There was a pause as they observed it

"It changed everything. Trade where there had been nothing. Worlds that had starved for a thousand years got rich in inside a generation." He was quiet a moment. "There are 31 known planets in the galaxy with Osmarine, and we're one of them. The miners are watched by soldiers, its one of the reason we're so––" he paused, "valuable."

In his schooling Burgundy had learned about Osmarine and its history of enabling galaxy connection, But only now, when the minister had said *83 years *did he connect the timing. 83 years was about the same timing that Dross had been under Nicholas' tribute arrangement.
So while interstellar travel pulled whole planets out of poverty, it also enabled new kinds of power and control, and made certain planets and their minerals more... *valuable. *

"What's this one" Burgundy said pointing to a small pillow on a shelf with a smooth sphere of a blue black rock sitting on it. The minister pulled it down and placed it in Burgundy's hand. It was heavier than it looked.
"Ultra-pure refined corvite"" He said as Burgundy stared.
"That," the minister said, "one crate of it, is worth more than a year of all the iron the northern fields pull out of the ground."
It was a well practiced line and the minister finished with a satisfied smile.
"Then why do we send it raw then?"
The minister's pleasure faltered for the first time. He glanced, quickly, at the King.

"We sell the ore. which by definition is Unrefined." the King said. He had not spoken since they came in. He was standing at the window with his back to them, looking out at the statue of his father from behind, and he spoke without turning around. "It goes off my ground raw and comes back at fifty times the price with somebody else's mark on it. I made my peace with that a long time ago. You will too."
"But why not refine it here?" Burgundy asked, handing the corvite sphere back to the minister "Build the refineries here. Build the processors here, and sell ––
"Stop!" the King said firmly.  "Because that is not what we are." The King turned from the window.
"We dig. We are very good at digging. We have been very good at digging for a long time, and it has kept us alive."
He paused, collected himself and said slowly "A man who is good at one thing and reaches for a second thing usually loses the first. Leave the refineries to the men who own the refineries."
The minister had recovered himself and moved them over to the table of ledgers. And they got to work reviewing.

After a short while Burgundy stopped listening to the report from the tin mines and looked out the window at the locals of Kettletown, filing moving through the square, the market that had changed his life just a few alley turns away.

And he thought. The processors sitting on the tables in the white room had, in all likelhood, been made from metal 10 kilometers away, then shipped to offworld foundries to be refined and fabricated and then sold all over the galaxy. Dross wasn't allowed to refine its own minerals, not allowed to make processors *because that's not who we are. *
So Dross ground the flour but wasn't allowed to make and sell the bread. It felt so wrong.

The meeting with the minister lasted two hours before the king, looking up to see Burgundy's sullen expression, stopped it. He walked over and put his hand on his son's shoulder, which he did rarely, and walked him down and back out into the cold, still surrounded by a wall of soldiers.
He walked Burgundy to the statue in the center of the square.
"Give us space," he said to the soldiers who widened their perimeter out of earshot.

"Look at him." He said pointing up to his father cast in metal. "He held this all together during his time.  And he did so not by trying to change it. We are not conquerors, Burgundy, we never were, whatever the sculptors want you to think. We are survivors.  and I don't think you understand how hard it is to survive here."
"No, sir."

"No. You don't, and that is my doing, and I am not sorry for it." He gestured down the slope at the low city. "This planet is begging to be invaded. Conquered. The raiders in every system around us would strip it to the rock if we didn't have guaranteed protection."
He was talking faster now. In a register Burgundy didn't recognize.
"It's a miracle he doesn't just conquer this place himself."
"Nicholas?" Burgundy asked. His father nodded. "Why doesn't he?"
"Because this works. For him and for us. And as long as we keep making it work, he gets what he wants, and we stay alive."

And the people down there, the ones who dig, they would burn the whole thing down if they ever got the chance. If they gathered and protested. That's what they want is to burn it down. And it is up to us to protect it. To protect all of it. "

He calmed his fast talking and then said in his more familiar lecture voice, "what I look at every day is everything that could go wrong here, at once,  and I hold it off by hand, every day. That's my craft. Soon it will be yours to hold"
He turned from the statue and looked at his son to see that the lesson had gone in.
Burgundy felt none of it.

Standing at the foot of the man who had held the line in his turn, hearing the whole case for the family laid out and every piece of it, he had to admit, probably true, he felt nothing lift in him. He felt cold. Not afraid, not moved.  ~~Cold, and tired, and aware of a pressure behind his ribs that had been building for weeks with nowhere to go, and that had lodged now, low and permanent, like a stone swallowed.~~

His father's world ran on keeping things small: men fed but never full, working together in the mines but not allowed to gather above ground. every warm room he had ever stood in paid for by a cold one below.
~~But in his white room, with the discs, and the machine that was getting better every night, nothing had to stay small for him to be warm or safe. ~~
"Thank you, Father," he said, convincingly

They were leaving the Custom House when the tribute master caught the King at the doors with a clipboard of papers that he handed to the king. The King read it without breaking stride and handed it back.
"South Twelve is short again?" he said, to no one. "Two collections running."
The tribute master started in about the depth they go. the challenges of mining corvite in those conditions.

"I don't need the reasons." The King was already moving into the light of the square. "I need the tonnage. Tell the governor he has until the next collection to right this. Third time short, he doubles the shifts and we arrest the crew chiefs, to great some urgency. "
He set a hand on Burgundy's shoulder, mild, instructive, the same hand that had steered him all morning. "You do not punish a shaft, Burgundy. You teach it to punish itself. That is the craft."

Burgundy thought of the one time he had stood at the rim of South Twelve, and the woman near the surface who had worked her stretch of rock and not looked up at him, the sweat on her that had looked permanent. Two collections short. One ship from now. He was learning to do that arithmetic without being asked.

They walked back across the square, the King ahead. Burgundy put his hands in his pockets and thought about his robot in the white room, the one that had learned that week to drive itself across the room and pick up a wrench. TK FINAL SENTENCE.

chapters.title: chapter 12 Festivals
paragraphs: The sun had arrived high in the sky. The warm months brought light and snowmelt to the strip of the planet people lived on.  From the castle you could see scrub trees leaf out over the landscape, growing thick even among the wounded landscape
Down the slope from the palace the snow had gone off the rusted roofs. No more smoke or stoves.

Somewhere in it a ladderfinch was singing. It was a small, tall red bird with black lines on its back that lived in the mines during the Freeze and came out only when the season changed. An omen of warmth that people here had used for thousands of years to test the air in the mines. A ladderfinch's song in echoing deep in the mines meant the air was clean, the mine was safe.

In the new light the Kings' Hall, illuminated in the high summer sun struck the great window in a new way,  casting hues of rust and deep vein-blue, laid across the grey floor thick as spilled paint.  Different stones than were illuminated during the Freeze months.
This morning the King walked into council in a cheerful mood.
"Morning gentleman." He said passing the morning tea chatter. "Festival today?"
By *Festival *he meant more ledgers. But these had line items like *grain spirits *by the barrel, *lamp oil,* *drum-hide*, *ten thousand scented candles* from offworld.
"Father I don't understand, what is this for" Burgundy said, now accustomed to asking questions in council
"The Festivals! The two big ones, The New Year Festival, during the Freeze, and The Midsummer Descent in six weeks from now."

As the meeting went on Burgundy learned that during these festivals, King opened the storehouses. Alcohol for every workers' quarter, paid from the royal accounts. Three days of suspended shifts. Music, lanterns, the great drum lines that Burgundy had heard from the palace walls his whole childhood, a low thunder rolling up from the city.

He remembered learning about the midsummer Descent. The ritual, his tutors had told him, went back to the Ghai, the mining people who had ruled Dross before his father's line, who marked the longest day by descending together into the oldest shaft to hang lanterns for their dead, to sing and drum and chant a cathartic chant and refusing to bring up a single stone that day, then followed by two days of feasting and lamp-lit processions, and folk music and spirit worship. Their marriages would happen during this festival.

Millions of people lived on Dross in conditions that anyone looking honestly would describe as slow grinding attrition, and twice a year the cities below the palace erupted into celebration so bright and loud it could be seen from orbit.
"Do you know why I pay for this?" The King said, glasses perched on the tip of his nose as he reviewed each line item, occasionally flicking his initials and turning the page
"No, sir."

"Because a man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has." His father signed the last line. "Remember that. This" he was nodding to the ledger, is cheaper and more effective than the army."
He went back to reviewing in silence and then,

"Men do not rebel in the weeks and months before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks and months after. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He set down the pen. "That is the craft, Burgundy. Nobody will teach it to you honestly but me."
Burgundy nodded the way he had learned to nod.

That night in his white room he was finishing the newest version of the robot's arms. He had taken the hand off it a week before and fitted a stub drill and a chisel point, so the arm could punch straight into rock or lever it apart along a seam. He had it practice on a patch of wall in the dungeons below Mira's wing and it worked decently well.

Then he taught it to grade itself. He wrote it two numbers to keep: how deep each cut ran, and how much charge the servos burned to move a kilogram of rock. It logged them every pass. And because he had also given it room to change one small thing between passes and keep whichever number came back better, it began, in the smallest way, to improve without him.

He watched it try a shallower approach angle, log the burn, keep the angle.  By the fourth night it was cutting the wall two degrees cleaner than the code he had given it, and the two degrees were its own improvement.  This was what the labs in the core world were doing. And here he was making it work on his own, just to the same degree.
And then it stopped getting better. He added a sensor to the drill head and it climbed a little and flattened. He rewrote the scoring function and it climbed a little and flattened.
A month of this adjusting and adding more and more sensors to the robot and still the robot was stuck in its ways.

One night he sat on the cold floor and watched the graph on his terminal flatten out. The machine could improve itself, but only in the small ways he had already built into it. Every real change still came from him, from his own hands, in the two or three hours a night he could steal. He had made a thing that could get better on its own and made himself the limit of how far.

The papers from the core world promised a world where the robot could improve itself infinitely. They had proven it could be done, at least theoretically. Not one, as far as he could tell, had implemented this in any real way. Maybe it simply wasn't possible.

chapters.title: chapter 13 The Preserve
paragraphs: in the days leading up to Midsummer, he went to the preserve with his Father.  The sun stood over the hills and would not come down and the brush country lay hot and dry under it.
The keepers were already ahead of them in the shimmer, walking the far grass, scattering grain for the animals to come and find.

He had left an experiment running all night. A paper had come up in the last crate describing code that would take in and compare visual data, and integrate methods that produced desired results. For him that meant, using the lenses and cameras in the new prototype's eyes so take a snapshot of every attempt at the rock and use that to improve itself. At least that was the idea. He had no idea how it was going because he was here at the sunny preserve.
His father had never taken him to the preserve. It felt like a kind of promotion in the king's trust.

This was the King's personal hunting ground that he had made when Burgundy was six. Built atop the land that used to belong to three villages, it was now totally overgrown with scrubby bushes, and tall grasses.
The party was small. The King, and Burgundy, and a governor of one of the western works, a broad giant of a man named Hald who laughed a beat ahead of his own jokes.

And two ministers. An old one from the treasury who said next to nothing and constantly coughed into a leather glove. And the security minister, Oz, a soft heavy man with a mild face, whom Burgundy had watched across the council table for a year now and never once heard raise his voice.
They walked through the brush, each with an impossibly old rifel slung over their shoulder.
Houses stood in the grass, or the halves of houses, their roofs long gone some of the walls dropped to knee height, hearths open to the sky.
And after ten minutes they came to a broken stone building at the edge of a wide clearing, roofless now, its walls green with moss and vines.
"The old village theater," Oz the security minister said, ducking through a gap that had been a doorway. "Before it was the King's ground. You get a view of the whole clearing from the top floor."

They climbed a stair with half its steps gone, up to what had been the second story, open to the sky now. The room had been cleaned and painted. It was smooth concrete and along the windows seven large red velvet pillows, oblong the length of a man's body. The man all went to the windows and lay down on the pillows, burgundy noticed that his was warm somehow.
Burgundy was now lying on his Belly next to Oz the security minister and all the men were looking out over the clearing. Surveying it quietly like men do.
Below and out ahead, the keepers were still at their work, walking the clearing in the morning light and scattering grain in a wide arc across it.
Then the keepers withdrew to the tree line, and they all went quiet, and waited, and quietly positioned their guns out the window.
A beast burgundy had never seen before wandered out into the open, nibbling at the grain.
"That's a Fen-buck," Oz whispered to Burgundy. "Bet you haven't seen one of those. They come from offworld, but we breed them here now. Best meat in the system"
The Fen-buck continued to graze along the field, unhurried, no vigilance in its posture.
Then it was down. A loud crack from the kings rifle had hit it in the neck and it dropped where it stood
A second wandered out of the brush, and then a third and forth, one with a large rack of antlers.
Oz took the second one, the group seemingly obeying some unspoken order of who shoots next.
"Your turn, prince," the King said. And all the men laughed.
He raised the rifle, set the buck's head in the sights, aimed a little high, and fired. The animal lifted its head, looked, and went back to the grain.
"First one's always high," the King said, and the men laughed. "Again, son."

He aimed and missed again, on purpose, and would go on missing. Something in him would not do it. Not here, not from a velvet cushion, not on ground where thousands of people had been ripped from their homes to make way for the kings entertainment once a year.
"You're thinking too hard son." Said the King. "We'll come back to you. Hald, go for it.
While the other men goaded Hald over his shot, Oz rolled onto one elbow and studied Burgundy a moment.
"Come down to the barracks some morning," he said. "I'll have a sergeant sort that aim out. Half a day. It's all breathing."
"Maybe I will."

"Do. It's good for the men to see you." Oz settled his chin back over his folded hands and watched the clearing. "Though I'll tell you what you'd see. Thin ranks. I'm stretched, prince. I have been saying so at council for two years, politely, which is getting me nowhere." He said it mildly. "Your father listens to you more than you think. If it came up, sometime, that the garrisons need men. There are ways to fill them. mandatory recruiting. We did that for decades when my father was in the army.  Men from the iron pits up north. theyre steady. Pliant." He paused one beat. "Uncomplicated."
Burgundy kept his eyes on the grass. "I suppose I never understood why we keep an army at all. The tribute protects us. That's what it's for."
Oz smiled without much moving. "Come now. A year coming to council and you're asking me why we keep soldiers?"
A long silence. And then,

"Well, it's not for the sky." Oz settled his chin on his hands. "Nobody's landing here. Nobody's raiding us. Nicholas has seen to that since before your grandfather. No, the sky's the one thing I never think about."
"Then what do you think about?"

"The ground." He said it like it was obvious. "The payment's got to come out of the ground, prince. Every month. You know how many shafts that takes, running day and night? Why do you think there's a night shift at all?" He picked something off his sleeve. "That's mine. Keeping the works working."
"Keeping them working," Burgundy said.

"Keeping things calm." Oz shrugged, a small motion on the pillow. "We keep a garrison in every mining town. Checkpoints on the shaft roads. My men walk the markets, the drink halls, the temple yards. Every day, everywhere, so it's never a question of whether the crown is watching. It just is." He resettled his chin. "We keep friends. In the shafts, in the housing rows, in the kitchens. Ordinary fellows. They take a little money, and they mention things to us."
"Mention things."
"Who's unhappy. Who's been complaining about wages or working conditions. Who's ungrateful.  Where people have been gathering after shift."

He might have been listing grain figures. "A man speaks against the crown in a drink hall, we hear it by morning, and he's down the hole by night. Quietly. No fuss for the neighbors. And the beautiful part is, after a while you barely need to take anyone. They take themselves. A man thinks twice with his own mouth. Cheapest soldier I have, prince, is the one inside every man's head."
"What is he filling your head with." The King had rolled over, grinning down the row at them. The men laughed on cue.
"Telling him about the groups," Oz said.
The laughter stopped being laughter. The King's face did something Burgundy had never seen it do, a small fast movement under the grin, there and gone.
"The one from last night?"
"yes. Third this month," Oz said. "Handled."
Burgundy looked between them. "What are the groups."

His father was quiet a moment, and when he spoke his voice had the patient, level tone he used on the council when a number was off. "There are men, son. Not many. Men who would take everything four generations built and burn it down. They live to sew disorder. They gather, in cellars, in back rooms, and they talk about stopping the mines. Stopping the mines." He said it twice, the way another man would say a blasphemy. "There were strikes, before you were born. You cannot imagine what a stopped shaft does to the arrangement. What it nearly cost us. So when they gather, we hear of it, and we go and fix it."

He looked back out at the grass. "I have kept this part from you. It is the ugliest corner, but a king spends more of his life on this than on anything in that hall, and you will too, so. Now you know."
Hald fired, and whooped, and somewhere out in the grass a fen-buck went down.
They shot for another hour. Burgundy lay on the velvet with the rifle against his shoulder and did not fire it, and nobody made him.

The grain scattered at dawn so the animals would come to the guns. The festivals paid for so the miners would come to the shafts. The listeners in the villages, the patrols, the groups unknotted in cellars. His whole life he had understood that Dross was poor, the way it was cold, a condition, a fact of the place. It was not a condition. It was maintained. The planet was held down and worked around the clock so the payment would go up on schedule forever, and everyone above a certain height on the hill spent their cleverness keeping it that way, and his father was not trapped in the system, his father was the system, and so was the mild man lying next to him, and so, in a coat he had never chosen, was he.
He thought about his robot, half built. And stayed locked on that image until––
"Son." His father, easy again, the grin back. "One more go at it. Hald's making you look bad."
"No."
It came out with an edge on it that surprised everyone, Burgundy most of all. The row of men went still. His father's eyebrows moved.
"I.. I don't feel well," Burgundy said, to the window frame, to no one. "The sun. I'll walk back."
He went down the broken stair alone.
The walk back was long and he did not notice most of it. Brush, then the fallen houses.

He stopped at one of them without meaning to. A threshold stone, worn hollow in the middle, smooth as a spoon, and grass growing up where the door had been. Three villages. His father had said it that morning the way he said hectares. People had worn this stone down crossing it, with firewood and buckets and children, for longer than the crown kept records, and then one year men with papers came up the road, and now fen-buck ate seed off the kitchen floors. And he knew where the people had gone. There was one place on Dross for the cleared-out to go, and it went down.
He walked faster after that.

Everything he passed attached itself to it. The keepers hauling the morning's kill to the wagon, men from the low city, paid to feed animals to richer men's guns. The wall of the preserve, built high and clean, better masonry than any house below it. And under everything, under the whole sunlit morning, the shafts running on shift, right now, this minute, men a kilometer down in the dark so that the ships would fill, and listeners among them taking coin, and his father up in a ruined theater on a velvet pillow calling it the craft.

By the time the palace wall came up out of the haze his shirt was stuck to him and he had stopped feeling the sun, and the thing in his chest was no longer an idea. It was a pressure, with heat in it, looking for a door.

It was midday when he came up past the great hall, and through the open doors the window was doing its Midsummer work, the sun standing so high and so long that the light came through the colored panes at an angle it held only a few days a year, laid out across the flagstones in narrow bright threads, the light shown through the pains of Corvite in ten shades of deep purple, ten of cobalt, reaching most of the way to the throne.  Servants had stopped in the doorway to look at it. Burgundy moved past without slowing
He went down through the corridors he knew

His mother's wing was quiet at midday, which was why she liked it. He came through the last door without knocking. She was across the room in the deep alcove between the shelves, up on the tall stool at her standing desk, a long brass lamp hung low from the arch above her so that she sat in her own small pool of gold, the forest-green door shut at her back, a pen in her hand.
She looked up.
She saw his face, and set the pen down.

chapters.title: chapter 14 The Library
paragraphs: She did not ask what was wrong. She sat on the tall stool in her pool of lamplight with the pen lying where she had set it, and she waited.

"How long have you known." It came out low, and then it stopped being low. "About the listeners. The men they pay in the shafts to report on their own crews. The patrols. The "groups", and what happens to them." He was moving now, back and forth through the edge of her light. "It is not a poor planet. It is a kept one. Kept poor, kept working, kept in the dark, so the ships fill on schedule, forever. He knows. Oz knows. Every man on that hunt knows."
She watched him and said nothing.
"And you knew." He stopped moving. "Twenty years. You've known and you've just sat here with your books and done nothing!"
The lamp hummed. His mother looked at him for a long moment, and there was nothing defensive in her face.
"There's mud on your shoes," she said.
"What?" he said confused
"You first hunt?"

"Yes my first hunt"  feeling frustration that she was changing the subject,  "And you what I saw?  How it works? They scatter grain to lure the animals out. That's the whole trick. Animals that are apparently bred not to fear anything, and who walk out into the open so they can shoot them where they stand. And in between shots they talk about the mines and the miners. And they tell themselves that the miners want chaos. They are are wreckers, people who want to burn everything down."
He was talking quickly, staring his mother in the eye

"So they spy on them, and arrest them for complaining about anything. And the festivals." He was louder than he had ever been at her, and he could hear it and could not stop it. "He pays for all of it so they get two good weeks. It's not generosity, it's a dose. Just enough joy that they can keep going, never enough that they start wanting more. It's just like the grain, Mother. It's the grain scattered in the clearing. It's a trap. Everyone up here seems to knows it, and you." His voice cracked on it. "You've known. Twenty years, you've been here knowing what they do and all you do is sit here with your books and hide from it all."
She let the words finish. She let the quiet come back all the way before she moved at all.
"Tell me something." She said quietly, followed by a pause.  "What did you lie on, up in the old theater, while you shot?"
"Pillows," he said. "Big red pillows."
"Eight of them," she said. "Each the length of a man."
"What does that have to do with--"

"They were sewn in this palace, the year the preserve was finished. You were six." Her voice did not change register at all. She might have been reading to him.  "Essa made them. Tuck's great-aunt, on his mother's side and a master seamstress. When your father's steward went looking for the finest hand on the planet he found her in a room behind a cook-shop, 85 years old, had been sewing since she was nine. He and brought her up here, to sew cushions for his hunting ground." A small pause. "She worked in the kitchens all that Freeze. I used to go down to the kitchens to visit you during the day when Tuck's mother was tending you during the day. And I met Essa. I would sit with her and watch her work. She would not talk while she sewed and I learned to like that. I was twenty-six and I had been on this planet eight years and she was only person other than Tuck's mother that I felt safe around."
Burgundy did not move.

"Essa had a bad cough, and it got worse that Freeze. So I started brining her medicine, stuff I get from offworld that the people down there have no access to. I would send her home with a bundle or remedies" She looked at her folded hands. "Then your father caught me." She took a deep breath, still looking at her hands.   "I had seen him angry before. I had never seen him like that. He yelled, and broke a vase against a wall. And called a meeting with my father saying that he's been violating the agreement by letting his daughter smuggle in supplies he didn't approve." She looked up at Burgundy. "Then he locked me in this wing for five days.  Servants brought meals. On the sixth day the door was opened and nothing was ever said about it again." She looked up. "Essa died before the thaw that year. But she finished the pillows first. They are very fine. You know, you saw them."
Somewhere in the silence a boiler coughed. A round of bird song fluttered by the library windows that were channeling bright sharp midsummer light.

"I am a prisoner here, Burgundy." She said it evenly, a fact among facts. "I am the seal on a treaty. My marriage was a business deal, and it holds whether I am happy or sad, so I decided a long time ago to stop keeping count of which I was." They looked at each other in the silence.  "And I didn't stop. Since that Freeze I've done what I can using my connections to help the people of this city. I still run the trade between Dross and my family. And with time your father stopped scrutinizing it. I've slowly found ways to get parts and supplies to the people. Stove parts. Fuel. Medicine. Books. Discs.  Slowly, because I learned the price of being caught. It's not just an issue between your father and me, it's between his family and mine."
She turned on the stool to face him fully.
Burgundy looked at her and felt the sensation he had felt the day she showed him her wing, that his understanding of his mother was expanding too quickly to process.

"And the biggest thing I've done for these people" she continued  "I've been doing for nineteen years." He nodding at him. "You were three the first time I took you to the royal engineer. He was designing a new mechanism for the palace clock and he would let you hold a tin of ball bearings while you watched him draw for hours.  I brought you back week after week. "
"And remember your toy room? There wasn't a single toy solider in there. I made sure your toy chest was full of tools, and old electronics you could take apart. Your father never went in there."

"And your education. While your rather wanted  you studying books and discs about the history of your father's line, I slipped in discs that taught you physics and math and computing logic. And from the time you were eleven you would study these discs on your own."

"And at night, before you could read, I used to tell you a story. The same one, over and over, because you demanded it. Great machines, bigger than the palace, coming down out of the sky onto Dross, and all of us walking up the ramps together, and the machines lifting us out into the galaxy. " She paused, looked down said more quietly, "Rescuing us."  She was looked up and him again "You would ask for that story night after night."
"Can't you see?  *You* are my answer, Burgundy."
He found he had to look at the floor.
"But do what do you want me to do?" he said finally.
"I don't know." She said it without apology. "That part is yours. You have the mind for it.  And from here it's for you to decide"

He crossed the room and sat down on the step of her alcove, below the stool, his back against the shelves, and looked from the mud from the preserve still on his shoes up to the expansive library, luminous with natural light. After a moment she came and sat next to him. And in the golden light, he rested his head against her should.

chapters.title: chapter 15 Osmarine
paragraphs: For the next six months he poured himself into the machines.

He had no plan. He knew that, and on the nights he made himself look at it squarely, it bothered him less than it should have. He had seen the realities of the regime that ran this planet, and he was inside that regime, wearing its coat, eating off its table, and the only answer he had to the discomfort was the pencil drawing pinned above his bench of a robot that could mine.
So he built.
Because the work was the one place the whole tangle went quiet.
Piece by piece, the pencil lines came true. He decided to build three new prototypes atop his sets of treaded tracks.

The body came first, low and broad on its treads, plated in the spun-carbon he had hoarded for a year. Inside it he stacked the new processor arrays, ten thousand times the little board that had run his first prototype.

A cluster of small spinning gyroscopes rode in the machine's core.  Springs and dampers folded into every joint, so that a shock from the rock was absorbed and measured. The machine could press against a surface and feel exactly how hard it was pressing. In the head he set two lenses a hand's width apart, so it could judge depth, like eyes.
It had been 18 months behind the yellow book, and his three prototypes were starting to look like something real. As tall as he was, looking at him through their thick lensed eyes.  Ready to work.
And after all this time and effort, he decided that Tuck's mom wasn't so wrong after all. That when you spend so much time with a inanimate object, it only feels right to give it a name.
He choose one inspired by the last name of the one of the Core world engineers who authored papers he read: Karz Dreck. He decided each robot would be called a DREKKO.
As the warm months ended and the Freeze started announcing its arrival, Burgundy's time in the white room turned to the DREKKOS' brains.

The array of advance processors in their chest could hold code tied all the hardware together: a program that took everything at once, the tilt and the torque and the temperature, the two eyes, the strain in every joint, and folded it all into one steady picture of the world, remade many times a second.

He had requested a disc containing everything the Central Library had on the history and methods of manual mining techniques in the galaxy, which he used to design arms. And this is what took the longest. But after 8 weeks of dedicated building the robots now had twin articulated arms on hydraulic mounts, thick as the trunk of a middle aged tree, and at the end of each a rotating head that carried its tools.
He had coded the whole thing, especially the feedback system based on what the discs taught him.
"Mining is a delicate art. Drill, pick, or chisel, each to its moment, the whole skill of it being to take the ore clean and waste nothing."  said one of the old books he read off his screen.

So the arms had a stub drill, a chisel point, a hammer face, a scaling claw, each one swappable, each one instrumented so the machine would feel the rock through them and choose the best tool for the job.
He spent three weeks on an experiment that made him slightly uncomfortable. Explosives.
It was a magazine of micro-charges, each one smaller than a marble, made to be placed by the arm into a drilled hole and detonated  precisely.

He machined the magazine, and the little launching cradle, and the arm's socket that would take it, and he loaded the charges in one by one with long tweezers. Then he stopped. He did not write one line of the code that would let the machine use it. He had never worked with explosives, and something in him balked at letting the machine decide when and how to blow something up. He took the loaded magazine off the arm and set it on the back shelf, behind the spare treads, where he could see it.
It was during those months that he moved his workshop.

The Freeze before, he had found a door in the underground portion of his mothers library that was sealed and painted over. When he pried it open he found a hall to an old dungeon and a gallery of prison cells centuries abandoned.

There were offshoot corridors that led to rooms he could not explain. One was a huge chamber walled in a smooth grey stone that was not the palace's. on the floos circular holes, the width of his arm. He walked over one and shined his lantern down and could not see the bottom. He could a breath of warm air coming out of the hole, where everything else held the cold of deep rock.
He hard studied in the school that the Ghai has used heat from the planet to fuel their society. Perhaps these holes were theirs.
He had been taught that the old kingdom under the palace were made up of endless tunnels and bunkers.
But these rooms were built to be lived in, for a long time, by people who had thought carefully about staying alive so far down.
And on one wall, cut shallow and sure and very old, was a mark he could not place: a circle within a circle, the inner one filled dark.
His mother's wing had been grafted onto this old dungeon and wandering through the old cells, along the rusted bars, he quickly noticed that he was surrounded by veins of mineral.

He knew from the maps he saw in the custom house that the palace's foundations sat directly on the shoulder of the southern ore country, and somewhere in the centuries, when power shifted hands, the new ruler had built the palace atop an old mine. There was still unmined riches here. Burgundy had tested the rock. And the sensor had come back with a reading he made it repeat three times.
Corvite.
A seam of it, thick as a room. A mineral that probably wasn't valuable when this was an active dungeon. It was, he understood, a small fortune sitting inside the palace's own foundations.

It was also, more usefully, the perfect teacher for his robot. Corvite was the hardest ore on Dross: dense, brittle in the wrong ways, prone to shattering into worthless gravel if the cutting angle was wrong by even a few degrees.  If the machines could learn corvite, they could mine anything on the planet.

So every night, after council, after the coat came off, instead of going up a ladder and through a book shelf to the white room, Burgundy went down through the previously sealed door, into the old dungeons and set his three prototypes against the wall, and watched it try.
He moved his terminal and array screens down here too. There was something comforting about being back in a basement working on robots again.

The DREKKOs tried their hand at real rock for the first time. And they didn't fail exactly. That was what made it hard. Each unit could bore into the seam. Each could strip freed ore into its bucket, sort waste rock by density. Watching them work, a foreman from the southern shafts would have wept. three machines chewing steadily into the hardest ore on the planet.
But there was a problem that threatened to end everything.
The machines were as tall as he was, and it worked the rock like a surgeon, but it could not dig.

The physics were not complicated. Push on anything and it pushes back exactly as hard. Drive a drill into a corvite face and the face drives the drill away with the same force, every gram of it. The great boring rigs in the deep shafts did not defeat that push with cleverness; they defeated it with mass, hundreds of tons of greyiron sitting on the drill bit cutting through the mountain.

But his machine had no mountain of mass to push with. He had built it light on purpose, and when it drove its drill into the seam at full thrust the whole beautiful body just slid backward on its treads, sensors reading perfectly, gyroscopes level, arms true, skating slowly away from the rock like a polite guest excusing himself.
It tried different angles. It tried bracing one arm while the other cut. It learned everything except the one thing it needed, which was weight, which could not be learned.
He sat against the cell wall in the green light from his terminal screens and watched his machine lose to physics.

The answer, when it came, came the way most of his answers came: off a disc, three weeks later, in a paper he almost skipped. It was a survey of core-world tunnel construction, dry, and buried in its middle pages was the fact that the tunnels of the core worlds were not cut by giants. They were cut by machines not much larger than his own. Each one carried, in a sealed housing at its rear, something that changed the whole equation: a sphere of refined osmarine.
He read the passage four times:

*"Advanced boring is achieved thought a refined antibarytic element, which exhibits inverse reactive displacement under load. Resistance encountered at the tool face is returned as proportional forward impulse, without recourse to platform mass. Industrial reports demonstrate signficant gains when the antibarytic element is maintained in magnetically suspended rotation, which  amplifies the anchoring effect by approximately three orders of magnitude.."*

The passage almost made no sense through the dense writing, especially because they were calling Osmarine an *antibarytic element. *But with some deeper research about the properties of Osmarine, his solution started to clarify.

Osmarine pushed the wrong way. Everyone knew that; it was the whole point of the stuff. But he had only ever thought of it as the thing that made ships light, the thing that kept doors in space open to allows travel between systems.

The tunnel engineers in the core world were using it for something totally different. As a brace. The harder the rock shoves the machine backward, the harder the osmarine presses it forward into the face. The rock's own resistance becomes the digging force. And spun inside a magnetic cradle, the paper was trying to say through the jargon, the effect multiplied a thousandfold, so that a machine that weighed one ton could bore into rock like a machine that weighed a thousand. The mountain's push, turned around and handed back to it.
He drew it out in pencil on thick sheets of paper. He did the math.
Everything he had built could stay. The machine did not need to be heavier. It needed a fist-sized piece of the strangest substance in the universe.
And there the whole thing stopped.

Osmarine was not just a mineral. It was *the* mineral, the one thing every power in the galaxy wanted. And even though raw osmarine was mined right there on Dross, it would not be easy to get refined.

But he knew someone who moved things you aren't supposed to have access to. His mother had moved medicine past a king. Her family moved cargo past whole navies. Somewhere in that grey river of hulls and manifests, there would have to be some osmarine that had slipped its count.

chapters.title: chapter 16 Mira's Shipment
paragraphs: At breakfast the next morning he found his mother at the small table by the east window, tea and a book, the way she sat before the palace woke. The morning was crisp and she was looking at the rising sun, one of the last before the Freeze would come and keep the sun glued to the horizon all day.
"I want to come on the next shipment," he said.
She closed he book and looked at him. "Why?"
"I've been taking from your family's shipments for a year and I've never once seen it. I want to know how it works." He sat down across from her. "And I want to meet your cousin."
She looked at him over the cup for a moment, reading him.

"Understanding the family trade is technically part of your princely duties," she said. "Your father would approve of the interest, if you asked him, which you won't need to." She went back to the book. "The next one is in three days. and Ressa may or may not be there."

Burgundy spent the next three days welding three cube chambers to his DREKKOS, preparing to house a sphere of Osmarine. On the third night his mother came by his chamber doors at dark and told him to follow.

They walked through the quiet palace lit by lanterns and toward the north gate, where a guard opened it without looking at either of them, then along a path running east, toward the low ground beyond the cargo field where the tribute loaded. Burgundy had assumed ships came down on Dross in exactly one place. But he had been wrong.

There was a second cargo field. Smaller. Lit only by amber lanterns set low along its edges. A freight ship sat on the landing pad, dark except for a few small utility lights no bigger than lamp-wicks.
This was not one of Nicholas's grey giants, which never landed at all. This was much smaller, maybe ten percent the size. It was scuffed, patched, resting on wheels. Its cargo ramp was down.
People dressed in dark clothing rolled crates up the ramp on dollies
Burgundy and Mira approached the ramp just as a woman was walking down it out of the ship to meet them. She was carrying a clipboard under her  arm.  Was this Ressa, his mother's cousin?

She held the slate out to Mira. "Manifest's ready. Ressa signed the outbound this afternoon.  The medicine order is short two pallets. The vendor's problem, not ours." So this wasn't Ressa, but rather one of her people.  His mother's cousin ran the trade without attending it. Then, with a glance at Burgundy that lasted no more than a half a second the woman said, "is this–"
"Yes" Mira said.
The woman snuck one more glance at Burgundy then turned back up the ramp signaling to the loaders to proceed.
Mira began focusing on the papers on the clipboard, scanning each line and occasionally signing her name.
Burgundy watched the ship.

Up the ramp went the crates of ore. He knew it by the markings now: density codes, grade markings, black corvite in sealed bundles. And beside the ore, in a separate stack the crews handled differently, more slowly, in padded cradles: casks. Small. Banded with metal. When a loader tilted one to seat it on the sled, the seam of the lid showed a faint glow, cold and steady.

He knew what it was. He had heard the word over the years. Mostly in a whisper: Cinder. A mind altering drug. The substance that fueled the spiritual dimension of the midsummer Descent. Refined from a rare deep seam mineral called Cindrite in a method the Ghai discovered. Fleks of the purified metal were ground with the tunnel mushroom and then consumed as a tea that glowed pale blue. Cinder was sacred in the old rituals but illegal in every system. And yet there was a black market for it throughout the whole galaxy. It was a stimulant that ran a man for two days and gave him blissful visions. This was Dross's second harvest, their metal cash crop that funded the Kings vanity projects, ~~now flowing up a ramp in casks bound for the black market run by his mother's family.~~
The casks went up, and the ore behind them, and Burgundy watched the it climb the ramp, and the question came out of him before he had decided to ask it.
"Do you trade osmarine?" he said to the women

Mira looked up from her clipboard at Burgundy and then to the woman, who laughed, once, before she remembered who she was laughing at. "Do we trade osmarine?" She shook her head. "Nobody 'trades' osmarine. The Alliance and Nicholas hold every gram between here and the core. There is not a fleck of it loose anywhere, and anyone who tells you different is a conman."
His mother was listening, not looking up from the clipboard.

"Nicholas has soldiers in the the four mines that harvest it on Dross," Mira said, "His own men, permanently, on our ground. They watch the miners, day and night, and at the ramp they weigh it to the gram, and it leaves on his ship and no others." She initialed a line. "So, no. We do not have access to osmarine."
Burgundy nodded, and looked back at the ship.
"What do you need osmarine for?" The woman on the ramp said
"Oh nothing, just curious how it works" Burgundy said and then stayed quiet as the shipment

Down the ramp came the arriving cargo. Burgundy had expected the incoming cargo to be illicit items like drugs or weapons. But instead he saw seed stock in heavy sacks. Casks of cooking oil, sacks of grain marked in a language he couldn't read. But also luxury items for the palace. Cooler crates likely full of special meats from other worlds. This stuff would end up on his plate at dinner. He had never wondered its origins.

after an hour of loaders going back and forth he saw a familiar stack of boxes of all sizes: Coils of special wire, drill heads wrapped in oiled paper, motors the size of fists nested in foam and what he craved most: the small wooden boxes he knew contained crystal discs from the Core world, packed tightly between wool and sawdust.

It was worrisome to have it all out in the open like this. The crew carrying his secret down the ramp on dollys like any other shipment. But when he really thought about it, he realized that to them this was just another crate. It may look suspicious to his father, but his father didn't ever come to these shipments. According to Mira, he hadn't for years. He preferred Mira to be the interface.
Mira looked at one of the crew and said "Lew." and nodded her head at the bundle of Burgundy's items.
Lew must have been the insider that Mira paid to get all this from the cargo field to the white room behind the bookshelf. He had no idea what kind of arrangement they had but he trusted it was safe.
Lew gave almost no acknowledgment that he had heard but went straight to gather the boxes and crates onto a motorized loader, and off he went into the dark.

Mira was finishing on the clipboard now. She initialed a line. She stopped at another. "This count is wrong. there were only 17 casks." The woman on the ramp checked; agreed. Mira corrected it herself, small precise figures, the same hand that labeled the toolbox drawers in the white room.

While she worked down the last pages he drifted to the rope line at the field's edge and looked out. The low city lay below in its scattered lights, small and warm against the dark, and at the very bottom of the slope, where everything else went black, one thin strip burned brighter than the rest.
The night market at the bottom of the city.

He could almost smell it from here, four years gone. The frying roots, the red spice. Tuck ahead of him in the crowd with his hands in his pockets. The singing cook, the heat of the fires and steam, the whole loud warm world of it going on down there right now without him.
And a scrap yard near the square, and a house full of jars and salvage, and Tuck's uncle coming down off a stool with a green corroded governor's core in his hand.
*You're underselling it,* he had said, fifteen years old, forgetting his accent. *It's worth ten times that. There's osmarine sealed in the core.*
*There's osmarine sealed in the core.*
He stood very still at the rope line.

The cage-lifts. No motor on Dross could haul tons of ore a kilometer straight up, so every cage carried a governor core bolted under its floor, a sealed housing with a little low-grade osmarine inside, canceling most of the load's weight so the winch lifted only the difference. He had known that since he was a boy. He had never once thought about what it meant.

Cores got knocked loose. And because they half-float, they would fall wrong, drifting sideways into old unused shafts. Gone forever, that is until miners would inevitably stumble upon them, and sell them to the local scrap yard. Ran.  Who stacked cores, thick with green patina, on a high shelf not knowing exactly what he had.
The most controlled substance in the galaxy was sitting in a junk man's house, priced as tin.
His mother closed the clipboard. The loaders were dragging the ramp chains loose.
Burgundy's gaze was fixes on the city below.
He was going to need to see Ran.

chapters.title: chapter 17 Tuck
paragraphs: During the Freeze, the palace turned back into a beacon of heat: every window lit, the boilers running day and night, and around its foundations a ring of bare wet stone where the snow could not lie. The only melted thing in sight.

The cold storage was the only cold room in the palace. Down in the wood-paneled cold room the size of a full bedroom, the walls wept frost and your breath stood in the air in front of you, the same as it did outside.

Racks ran floor to ceiling on three walls. Sacks of tubers, wheels of hard cheese, stout crocks of butter stacked like masonry. A whole shelf of desserts waiting on their plates, custards and dark tortes glazed to a shine. 
And along the back wall, on iron hooks, the fen-buck from the preserve, skinned and split and hanging in their parts, shoulder and haunch and saddle, each piece still keeping the shape of the animal it had been.
Burgundy waited at the back racks, behinds wheels of cheese.
he only waited ten minutes before Tuck entered and went to the fill a basket with yellow onions.
"Hey. Tuck burgundy said as he stepped out from behind the rack.
"What the–––" he squinted into the dark "Ghost? Is that you? What in the––"
"I need your help Tuck."
Tuck's face softened to something familiar to Burgundy. And he smiled
"Oh man, Ghost, you're up to something *again?"*
"Yes"

"What? more robots? Still?" He laughed a big laugh and Burgundy smiled. "You're still doin' that even though you've become all princely now? Man I thought you were done. That you were done forever. I see you going to the big meeting every morning. Hunting with the men? Even the kitchen heard that you missed the buck twice. I figured you just didn't wanna shoot one."
"Tuck," Burgundy said. "I need to visit Ran"

Tuck let out a breath that hung white between them. Then he laughed again. "Man sorry, Ghost, I just can't believe it. Can't believe you're here. Not gunna lie, I grieved you man. Thought you had changed forever and turned into one of them." Burgundy had never heard Tuck talk about his family as *one of them* but he now understood why he would.
Tuck re-shoudlered the sack of tubers he was carrying out and said "yeah course I'll take you to Ran's. Securities a bit trickier than when we used to sneak about. But I have a way"
"Thanks Tuck. I really appreciate it"
"Course, let meet in the old wine cellar on the full moon, five days from now. The guards always get drunk on the full moon. I'll make sure they the get the strong stuff this week"
Burgundy nodded and Tuck started back up the stairs toward the warmth. "And Ghost," he said on his way up "really good to see you again."
"You too Tuck.
Five nights later Tuck and Burgundy met up in the basement.
"Ok we're going out the service entrance, where we get our food shipments. I'm gunna put you in one of the big long wooden crates the cheese wheels come in, and dolly you out of the gate"
"And the guards?"
"Remember, they're drinking tonight, I personally delivered some barley liquor that will have them laughing at the full moon when we pass. They won't ask to check anything"
Tuck's plan worked exactly has he envisioned. Soon Burgundy was climbing out of the wooden crates on the side of path that lead from the palace to the town.

The path lay in the long dusk of the Freeze, the sun somewhere behind the hills where it would stay for months, the snow holding the last of the light. The full moon did the sun's work, throwing their shadows blue across the drifts. They walked quickly, collars up, boots squeaking on the pack.
"So what's all this prince business, then," Tuck said. "Meetings every morning. Hunts. The coat."
"It's an act."
"An act."

"It keeps my father not asking questions. Or ever knowing what I'm actually doing" He watched his breath go up. "Which I'm not going to tell you about. The less you know, the less danger you're in. You're in enough just walking me down this hill."
Tuck stopped walking for a second. "Danger? Endanger?" He caught back up. "What are you doing, Ghost? How serious is this thing?"
Burgundy said nothing.

They came into the low city through the night market. Burgundy wore the same laborer's coat, a scarf up over his face, and through the wool the smells came anyway, the frying roots, the red spices, the smoke off the stone ovens, and for a few steps he was thirteen again and the whole warm loud world was his to walk through.
Nobody looked at them. The Freeze kept every head down and every scarf up. Being nobody was easy in the cold.

Ran's yard sat where it had always sat, the heaps taller under the snow, the paths between them beaten to ice. Tuck knocked, and pushed the door open on the same stove-warmth, the same pepper pot, the same walls of jars.
"Uncle. Brought a customer."
Ran came out from the back room wiping his hands on a rag. He saw tuck and started to smile. Then Burgundy pulled the scarf down.
Ran went still. The rag stopped moving in his hands. His eyes locked on Burgundy's face.
"Tuck." His voice was careful. "What is this."
"Uncle, it's fine, it's––Ghost you weren't supposed to––"
"I'm here to buy," Burgundy said. "That's all." He nodded at the high shelf, at the basket sitting where a basket had sat for four years. "The governor cores. All of them."
Ran looked at him a long moment. Then he barked, once, half a laugh and half something else, and dug two fingers into his vest pocket, and came out with a coin, and slammed it flat on the counter.

"I knew it." He left his finger on the coin. It was old and rubbed and it had the Burgundy's face on it, stamped young. "You paid me with that a coin just like this, four years back. And after you walked out of here talkin' like a book with your fancy accent, I sat with it under the lamp, and I looked at the face on the coin, and thought I was mad." He took his finger off it, his face locked in a furrowed brow.
