He got the stool and lifted the basket down, one-handed, far too easily, the way no basket of metal should come down, and set it on the counter where it sat a little too lightly. Twelve spheres, each the size of a big man's fist, crusted green with age, and where the crust had flaked away, thin veins of some translucent metal ran through the shells, catching the lamplight like frozen water.

"Twelve now," Ran said. "After what you said that day, I put word down the shafts. Any man finds one of the floaters in the old workings, drifted off into some shaft where it's got no business, bring it to Ran, Ran pays fair."

He turned one under the lamp, not quite letting it go. "Never cracked one. Don't really know what I'd do with low grade osmarine.  But I collected 'em, on the word of a boy I met once." He set it back and looked up, and the wariness came back into his face. "And now the boy's back. And I gotta say I'm not feelin' too great about selling you a prohibited substance at the moment"
"Uncle," Tuck said. "Come on. He's not going to do anything bad with them."
"You told me yourself he'd gone all royal. Sittin' the meetings. Doin' the hunts n' all. Your words, Tucks, not mine."
"Yeah, I thought that. It's not real. It's a show he's putting on."
"And how would you be sure of that."
"Because" Tuck paused "I know him," he said looking at Burgundy with an expression that felt like home.

Ran looked at his nephew a moment. Then Burgundy took the sack from inside his coat and set it on the counter and opened the neck of it. Gold, his father's face over and over in the lamplight. A pile of coins, surely more than the yard turned in a season.
Ran looked at the money and did not touch it.

"I'll ask you one thing straight," he said, " What are you buildin'. Because if it's some new way to hold this city down, we're full up. You understand me? It can't be held any harder than it's held. They took Nate two days back. My friend thirty years. Down the hole. For months probably, " Ran's anger was igniting.

"And you know what for? Talkin'. On shift, to his own crew, about the state of the lower shafts, Dismal working conditions. And someone on that crew rats him out, and just last night he was thrown into the hole." He wiped his hands on the rag again "That's what it is here now. Every man watchin' his own mouth. So you tell me what you're buildin', or the basket goes back on the shelf, gold or no gold."
"It's not for control," Burgundy said.
"So says the crown prince in my shop."
"My father doesn't know I'm here." Burgundy said it flat.  "And I'll tell you what else he doesn't know, because he's never once asked. He doesn't know TKTKTK

I've sat there for almost two years listening to the men who run this planet talk about you and your neighbors like a herd of animals that needs to be fenced. And I've sat there and said nothing, because saying something up there actually fixes nothing down here." He looked at the basket, and then back at Ran. "Everyone in that palace spends their cleverness keeping this city exactly where it is. I'm spending mine another way. That's as much as I'll tell you. Now are you selling these cores or now?"

The stove ticked. Tuck had gone quiet. Ran looked at Burgundy for a long time, the way he had once looked at a boy pricing scrap, and whatever he was searching for, he must have found some of it, because he pulled the sack of gold toward him without counting it, and tipped the twelve cores one by one into a grain sack, rags folded between them so they would not knock.  He pushed it across the counter.
"Make something worth what it cost," he said.

chapters.title: chapter 18 Digging
paragraphs: He had the cores for a week before he found the nerve to crack one.

They sat in the grain sack Tuck had dollied through the gate, twelve of them. And every time he passed the bench he picked one up and set it down again. Fist-sized, crusted green, lighter in the hand than a thing that size had any right to be. He knew what the lightness was now. He had read the passage off the disc until the dense core-world words came apart in his mouth: *a refined antibarytic element, resistance at the tool face returned as forward impulse, no platform mass required, the effect amplified when the element was held spinning. *Ran had called it *the stuff that floats*.
So he sawed one open, cutting through the tin until the two curved halves fell open. And inside it, an ivort white sphere, mounted into a cradle with a spinning mechanism.

There was already a small perfect hole drilled through the center of the sphere. Where the spinners could grip it. He mounted the sphere into the cage he had welded, onto the back of the DREKKOs, the cage now clad with magnets, He flipped one switched inside the cage and the sphere started to spin inside the mount.   The report had called this moment *magnetically suspended rotation.*
He walked wheeled this first DREKKO over to the corvite face that had thrown it a week ago, the same seam, the same chisel point set true along it. Current on.
He gave the drive command.

The treads stood still on the stone as the machine started pushing forward into the rock. The reaction that used to push the machine backward, now went up the arm and into the spinning sphere of osmarine and back down into the bit, and the chisel walked into the rock instead. A wafer of corvite the size of his thumb split off along the seam, dropped, and rang once against the floor of the robot's empty bucket.
He sat down on the cold floor where he had watched it lose so many times, and listened to the drill go on into the rock, and for one long breath it was the finest thing he had ever made.

He spent the next week rigging all three of his DREKKOs with osmarine spheres in the cage he wleded inside their chest. He rigged two per robot and calculated that this increased each DREKKO's mass by seven thousand percent.
As he put the robots to work on the wall, he started to notice what would become his final challenge: The robots got stuck.
As he put the robots to work on the wall, he started to notice what would become his final challenge. The robots got stuck.

He saw it first on a single machine, on a night he was too tired to intervene. It had found a seam, set the chisel  along it, and begun to work, but the seam was not giving. A harder machine had never existed on this planet. It drove the point in with the force of something fifty times its size, and the corvite held anyway, the way corvite sometimes did, and the machine's answer was to do it again. Same point, same angle..

He sat against the wall and watched it strike that dead seam forty times, patient as a clock, and understood that it would strike it four hundred times, four thousand, all night and into the morning, because nothing in it could conclude the one thing a twelve-year-old shaft boy would have concluded in a minute: this seam is done, move on.
And once he had seen it in one, he saw it in all of them.
They could sense everything. The two eyes read the face and picked the tool and set the angle, and the code he was proudest of scored every action as it happened.
But the data wasn't coming back to improve the code. They could grade their own work and could not learn from the grade, could not do more than the few blunt adjustments he had written in by hand.
And so each machine climbed for a week or two and then settled onto a competence that never became mastery.

Every real improvement still ran through him, his read of the log, his rewrite, his upload, one tired hand feeding data and feedback to three tireless bodies. All the force the osmarine gave them, and they spent it doing the same wrong thing harder.

He knew, from the discs, that he was not the only one stuck here. Three labs in the core worlds had been circling this exact problem for years. How to build a machine that did not just sense and score but *learned*, folded every action back into itself, so that each swing taught the next swing and the improving itself improved.

The papers agreed it was coming. The papers had been agreeing for a decade, from inside clean labs, on simple rigs, in air scrubbed of dust and heat. Nobody had cracked it there. He certainly had not cracked it here.
He shut the machines down one at a time, and the cell went quiet, and the seam the first one had been worrying all night stood in the lamplight, barely scarred.
The strongest digging machines ever built on Dross. And worth nothing, none of it, until they could teach themselves to get better.

chapters.title: The Lounge
paragraphs: His father had never once asked him into the lounge.
It sat off the private wing, a long room Burgundy had walked past a thousand times and entered never, until tonight.

The first thing he noticed was the light. Most of it came from lanterns with amber shades set low along the walls, so the whole room stood in a honey-colored glow that rounded the edges of everything and made the leather chairs shine like chestnuts. Between the lanterns, on low tables and in wall brackets, hung globes of corvite ground thin enough to pass light, each a different shade, one the blue-black of a deep bruise, one nearly violet, one the green of pond ice, glowing cold and small against all that warm.

The carpet took his boots to the ankle. The cushions heaped in the chairs were velvet, deep red, stitched in a fine close hand he knew, though it took him a moment to place it, and when he placed it he wished he had not. Essa's hand. The old woman had sewn for this palace until the Freeze took her, and here was her work, propping up the men who ruled the planet.

His father sat in the largest chair with a glass at his elbow, and Oz sat across from him, and each of them held a cigar of a leaf Burgundy had never seen, rolled thick as a thumb, the wrapper a dark green gone orange at the edges with a thread of gold running its length.
The smoke came off it heavier than woodsmoke and sweeter, and hung in the amber light in slow blue sheets.

"These come from a jungle world in a different system", his father said proudly about his cigar "A place that grows a hundred leaves and every does something different you." He laughed and looked at Oz who chuckled along.  He waved at a box of them on the table. Burgundy did not take one.
"Sit," his father said, pleased. "You're old enough now to join us from here for out little...chats." He smiled at Oz.

The King had invited Burgundy tonight promising that this was the *real council,* where the real decisions about security were made. And then he gave a speech about *developing discernment over where formality and process actually hinder progress. *
So he came, and sat and he listened.
Oz talked the way he moved, without hurry. But his voice picked up urgency when he gave the king the update on the security situation.
"More groups tonight," Oz said. "The south this time. Bolder than I'd like."
"Bolder how," the King said.
"There's talk of a stop-work. Three of the deeper levels." Oz said.  "Messages passed at shift change, world of mouth. Nothing written. "
The word sat over the table. Nobody at council had said *strike* in Burgundy's lifetime, and Oz did not say it now.
"We have a minder down there. He reported it right away and we took care of it. We took two or three of the offenders.

"It's always a few," his father said, comfortable, turning the cigar in his fingers. "A few who would rather pull the whole roof down than carry their share of it. The rest are good. They want to feed their families and be left alone. Our work is to see that the few never teach the many to be so full of hate and resentment." He said it kindly, and Burgundy sat on Essa's cushions in the honey light and felt a new feeling that was becoming familiar to him, the one from the preserve, from the grain scattered in the clearing.
Then, gathering his papers, as an afterthought: "Oh, and we took one more tonight. A scrap dealer, up in Kettletown. He was selling osmarine."
The King's head came up. "What.?"
"Osmarine, sire. Low grade, but real."
"How does a Kettletown junk man come by osmarine."
"Governor cores." Oz squared the pages against the table. "The lift cores. The ones under the cage floors, that carry the harvest up the shafts. He was sawing them open for what's inside."
"And how are lift cores ending up in a scrap yard."

"They get knocked loose, from time to time. A cage slams, a coupling goes, and the core drops off and drifts away into the dead shafts. It's not new. What's new is that this man had put a call out saying he'd pay a good price for any found floaters."
"Floaters. And who was he selling the stuff to?"
"That we haven't found." Oz laid a folded paper on the table. "But he'd done well for a junk man. There was a strongbox under his floor. Fresh-minted gold."

His father picked up the paper, read it, set it down. The good humor had gone flat out of his voice. "Someone is buying loose osmarine off a Kettletown scrap man," he said. "I don't know who, and I don't know what for, and I dislike both of those. Find me the buyer."
There was a silence while the men puffed their cigars.
Burgundy sat very still in the honey light. hit heart was going so hard he was sure the thud of it was visible through his shirt.

They had Ran. Ran was in a hole somewhere in the dark right now. And they were looking for the buyer and the buyer was him.  Would ran tell his interrogators that the prince showed up with freshly minted gold and bought twelve governor cores?
He needed to move. He needed to get up from this chair without running.

He made himself count ten. Then he set his hands on the arms of the chair and said he was tired, that council came early. His father waved the cigar in a small arc that was half blessing and half dismissal.
"Go to bed. You did well today.  You listened, that is most of ruling." He was already turning back to Oz.
Burgundy walked out of the lounge at the pace of a tired prince, down the corridor and around the corner, and then he was running.

He went down the back stairs two at a time and through the cold rooms and came into the kitchens still in his good coat, and a dozen faces lifted from their work and went still. It was late. A few of them were left, scrubbing the long tables. They looked at the prince standing in their doorway breathing hard with something wrong in his face, and none of them said anything.
He looked around for Tuck who was at the sink, just looking over his should.
paced across the kitchen and Burgundy and pulled Tuck by the sleeve and pulled him out into the passage, where the stone was cold and the light was thin.
"They took Ran," he said.
"I know," Tuck said.
It stopped him. "You know?"
"Word came up an hour ago. His neighbor's boy runs the milk to the east gate." Tuck's face was concerned and scared.

"It's because of me." The words were out before he could weigh them. "He collected the cores because of me. I told him what they were worth, four years ago, and he believed me and put the word out and gathered them, and I went back and bought every one, and tonight they came for him." The corridor held still around the two of them.
Tuck did not tell him it was not his fault. That was the thing Burgundy would remember, later, in the dark. Tuck had never been in the business of comfortable lies, and he did not start now.
"Is there anything you can do to get him out?" Tuck said. Burgundy knew there wasn't.
"I...I don't know Tuck" he said shaking his head.
They looked at each other in silence a long moment.
Burgundy went back up through the palace to his own wing, past the guard who did not look at him, and shut the door of his chamber, and lay down on the bed in his clothes.
He had thought of it as his. His secret, his risk, his machines, a thing that touched no one but himself. But it wasn't just him anymore.

The weight of what he had done came down on him in the dark, and for the first time since the yellow book swung open on the white room he did not think about the machines at all. He turned his face into the pillow and cried, quietly, so the guard outside the door would not hear.

chapters.title: chapter 20 Closed Loop Embodiment
paragraphs: He did not sleep. He lay in his clothes on the bed where he had cried himself empty.
Then he went over the problem again. Every version ended the same way.

He could not go to his father. If he asked the King to release Ran, his father would ask why the prince cared about a scrap dealer in Kettletown. The answer would lead to the hidden bookcase, the white room, and the two years Burgundy had spent buying parts in secret.
When Burgundy could not solve a problem, he worked.

So before the clock struck midnight he spring out of his bed and rushed through the dark palace toward his dungeon-turned-lab where he had been circling the same problem for weeks.  Robots that would not teach themselves to improve.

A new batch of discs painted a picture of Core-world teams in top labs, three of them, working the same problem from different directions. How they had begun successfully testing robotics whose own sensors fed the machine's own learning.

Every strain gauge and thermal reading and torque curve pouring data into the code's scoring functions in real time, the way a hot lantern teaches a child's hand: touch it once, and the brain rewrites itself so you never touch it again.

The papers called it *closed-loop embodiment*. He had read the twelve of them until he saw the code in his sleep. And somewhere in the reading he had understood something: These researchers had proved all this only in clean labs, on simple rigs, in air scrubbed of the dust and heat and the physics that made his machines choke.

None of them had ever spent a night on their back under a machine with sealant on their hands. They were brilliant but they were blind to what they called in the papers: *Real-world industrial application scenarios.*
All he had to do was implement their theories into reality and he would be ahead of them.
He could feel he was arriving at a final frontier. And he could feel that whatever this meant, it would result in some way to free Ran. Or at least ensure his safety until they could let him out.
So he worked the problem.
The sensor buses that fed data from the machine's arms to its brain had been built, by him, in a different life, to report their readings on a fixed cycle to a fixed log.

Now the new learning loop program needed them raw and constant, like a firehose instead of a faucet, a waterfall of real-time data, as constant as human senses flowing into a brain. So with a few lines of code and some rewiring, he opened them up.

But every time he opened the data channels all the way, the processors drowned. The scoring functions fell behind the sensations they were meant to score. The machines got clumsy, worse than before, drunk on their own feeling, and twice that night a drill arm slammed a cutting head into the corvite at an angle that sent shatter pinging off the gallery walls like shrapnel.
He replaced an arm, twice that night. He had done it twenty times by now.

He throttled the flow and it went dull. He batched it and it went blind. He let the machine choose its own sampling rate, which the second paper had hinted at and the third had warned against, and the third paper was right, in a way that cost him a hydraulic line and an hour on his back under the second prototype with sealant drying to a crust on his hands.
Somewhere past the fourth hour he stopped being careful, and he knew he had stopped, and he let it go.
There was a mode he went to when it got late, that he did not trust and could not do without, where the experiments stopped being designed and started being thrown.

He recoded the buses on all three machines in configurations he would not have tried rested, and wrote scoring variants faster than he could test them, and queued them to run in rotation, each machine scoring itself and passing what it learned sideways to the other two.
Then he did the thing he had promised himself he would never do.

He took the micro-charges down off the back shelf. He had built them a year ago, a magazine of little explosives the size of beads. Each one meant to be set into a drilled hole and fired to pre-fracture the rock.

These had been too dangerous to him previously but tonight the thing that balked was gone. He fed the dispensers like a cartridge into a slot in the arm and programed their use. He set bounds on the frequency of the charges, and checked the bounds twice, because he was not interested in blowing up the foundations of the palace.

The slit window had gone warm and sharp. Dawn. Council in two hours, and he had not slept. He looked at the three machines idling against the black seam, their green panels pulsing, the queue loaded and waiting on his word, everything he knew and half of what he only guessed set loose at once with no hand on it.
"Go," he said to himself, and pressed the key, and left them working.
He did not look back at the wall. If he had, there would have been nothing to see. Three patient machines, a barely wounded vein.

Council was a blur he moved through with his body while his mind stayed forty feet down, in two places at once, the ran's cell and the seam hi Robots were working on armed with a hundred new experiments.

He got through the grain reports. He got through a dispute between two southern governors. Twice his head dipped, as we nodded off, chin to chest, and the second time he surfaced to a silent room and his father looking at him down the length of the table.
"Am I boring you."
"No, sir. I apologize. I was reading late."
"Reading?"
"The northern field reports." The lie arrived without being sent for. Two years of practice.
His father studied him a moment, then let it go, and Burgundy breathed out slowly, the way you bleed pressure off a line, and under the table his hands would not stay still
"Read earlier" the king said.

It was tribute day. The ships came down at midday. He stood on the platform at his father's right hand and watched Nicholas's ships arrive out of the white sky, three of them, each the length of the palace and its grounds laid end to end. The stopped to hang in the air hundred meters up without wings, without any visible propulsion. Just a deep low pressure that Bunrgundy could feel in his molars.

White arms unfolded from the ships' bellies, joint after joint after joint, and began lifting the thirty-tonne crates in gentle clusters, a month of the planet's blood rising into holds that never showed their insides.

He was so tired the membrane between his two lives had gone to nothing. The day-prince stood in his coat and the night-builder counted joints and thought, helplessly, that if those arms had a feedback loop they would teach themselves to nest the clusters tighter and shave a second off every lift and then a second off the shaving. And behind that thought, the whole time, sat the three machines against the seam and the small sick hope that the explosives had not brought the foundation down, and behind that, Ran.
His head dipped.
He caught it, half a second, and came back to the pressure-hum and the white sky and found his father looking at him. Not with anger. That was the strange thing.
"You're tired," the King said, quietly, under the hum.
"Yes, sir."
His father turned back to the field, and was silent a while, and then, still watching the ships:

"You've become a great prince. I want you to know I see it. You'll be king someday, sooner than either of us would like, how fast years are going. And for the first time I believe you're ready for it. More than ready." He paused. The arms folded themselves away, joint after joint, into the bellies of the ships. "I'm glad you gave up those childish things. The tools and the wires. I know it wasn't easy, but look at you." He nodded at the field, at the order of it, the minerals rising into the sky on schedule. "This suits you. This is right for you. This is what you are."
The ships went up the way the sun crosses a sky, without seeming to move, and were gone. The pressure lifted out of his molars. The cargo field was empty.
"Thank you, Father," he said.
It was, he thought, walking off the platform at his father's side, the kindest thing his father had ever said to him.
He was released an hour before dusk, and by the last of his three routes through the old corridors he was running, coat over his arm, taking the worn stairs down by memory.
He smelled it before he saw it.

Rock dust. In the hallway. Thick, a mineral fog hanging in the light of his lamp, and under it a smell he knew from exactly one place in his life, the rim of a working shaft. Blasting residue. Deep rock, opened.
He came around the last turn into the cell-turned-lab and stopped.
The wall was gone.

chapters.title: chapter 21 Tunnels
paragraphs: Not damaged. Not advanced upon. *Gone*.

Where the seam had been, where a year of patient insufficient chewing had left a shallow scarred tunnel there was now a hole. A real tunnel. Round-shouldered, clean-walled, taller than he was, driven straight into the rock, and so deep that his lantern simply failed inside it, the light falling into the dark the way a stone falls into a well.
The three prototypes were nowhere to be found.

Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel for a long moment, listening to his own pulse beating in his neck, and then he did the thing that years of discipline had built into him: he went to the terminal.
The logs were still streaming across all three screens.

He read standing up, then sitting, then leaning into the screen with both hands on the desk, scrolling, not breathing right. The queue of reckless experiments had run in rotation, as designed, for the first two hours after he had left, variant after variant failing in the old familiar ways, drowned processors, drunk actuators, one logged shatter-event that had cost the second prototype a cutting edge. And then, in the third hour, one configuration on the third machine, one of the ones he had wired past midnight and could barely remember, had *caught*.
Caught was the only word for it. He watched it in the logs the way you watch a spark take to dry grass.

The data firehose and the scoring loop had synchronized. Not throttled, not batched, but brought into rhythm, the machine sampling its own body in rhythm with its own actions, feeling each cut as it made that cut. And the performance line, the line he had been tracking for years, had bent upward.

Then the third machine had passed the configuration sideways to the other two, as designed, and all three lines had bent, and then the loop had begun doing the thing the papers promised could happen but never achieved outside a lab, and Burgundy had never once seen with his own eyes:
It improved the improving.

Every second, the logs said, each machine was taking in its thousands of tiny sensations, torque flutter, thermal bloom, the acoustic signature of rock about to shatter versus rock about to yield, and converting them into micro-adjustments: a cutting angle shaved by a tenth of a degree, a charge from the micro-dispensers placed not where the rock was weakest but where the *next three cuts* would want it weakened, the blast so small and so exact that it did the work of an hour's grinding in a sound no louder than a knuckle crack. And each adjustment fed the next. And the rate of adjustment was itself adjusting. The performance curve in the logs was no longer a line bending. It was a line skyrocketing.
He looked at the numbers at the bottom of the stream, tonnage, waste ratio, energy per kilogram, and he did not believe them.
Then he took his lantern and raced into the tunnel.
The tunnel was beautiful. That was the thing he had not expected. The walls were not rough-bored but *finished*, cut in long smooth strokes that overlapped like the grain of planed wood.

And at intervals along the floor, in neat staged rows, sat the ore. Processed. The machines had not just cut the corvite free; they had pulverized the waste rock and packed it into the walls, leaving a smooth finish. And the corvite itself they had crushed, graded, and pressed into dense dark bundles the size of bread loaves, wrapped in sheeting from their own supply spools and stacked with a regularity that no human crew on Dross had ever achieved or attempted.

He picked one up. It was heavier than it looked. It was worth, at the prices he now knew by heart, more than a southern miner earned in half a year, and there were dozens of them, staged at intervals.

He walked on. The tunnel dipped, and turned, following the vein. He could see where the machines had made choices, where the seam had forked and the cutting pattern showed a moment of exploratory nibbling before committing,  and he had gone perhaps three hundred meters, far beyond any map of the palace foundations, when the character of the walls changed, and he stopped.
The machine-cut smoothness ended at an edge as clean as a doorway.  Beyond it, the tunnel was still a tunnel, but an old one.
Old was not the word. The walls beyond the breach were hand-cut, pick-scarred, the scars softened by centuries of seeping water until they looked less carved than grown.
Water dripped somewhere ahead, a slow mineral music, and the air that moved out of the dark against his face was cave air, wet and unbreathed.
His lantern found the ceiling: soot stains, ancient ones, the ghosts of torch brackets. And on the wall beside the breach, at shoulder height, where a man resting his hand would find it:
Engravings.
He brought the lamp close. Rows of figures, cut shallow and sure: miners with picks, rendered in the blunt confident strokes of people carving their own lives.

And above the figures, repeated, a mark he knew. He had seen it in exactly one place before, in the oldest of the palace's history books, in the chapter every tutor hurried through: a circle within a circle, the inner one filled dark.
The mark of the Ghai.
He stood in the dripping dark with his lamp on the old stone and his education came back to him in pieces.

Before the current line, before his father's family, before the tribute, before Nicholas, there had been a kingdom on Dross, and it had lived *under* the planet rather than on it. The Ghai. A mining people whose answer to a lawless sky had been depth. No walls, no fleet, no army But a thousand kilometers of tunnels, and a capital no raider ever found because it had no outside.
The histories his tutors taught said the Ghai had faded, collapsed, dispersed, were conquered. Something. He didn't remember.
But he did remember that their tunnels had been filled in centuries ago, sealed for safety when the palace was raised on the ruins of their mines. *Filled in.*
He remembered the phrase exactly, remembered the tutor's voice saying it, because even at ten years old he had thought: *who would fill in a thousand kilometers of tunnel? Who could?*
No one, was the answer. No one had. They had sealed the doors and written *filled in* in the books, and the books had become true because no one checked.
His machines had just checked.
He should have gone back. He knew he should have gone back. The logs alone were a life's work, the bundles in the tunnel were a hoard.
But the dark ahead of him was pulling with the specific gravity. And somewhere in that dark, faint and rhythmic in the silence he could hear his machines.
He followed the sound.

He walked for what might have been an hour, down through the labyrinth of the old kingdom, his lantern a small moving room of light in a blackness. The tunnels branched and rejoined. There were rooms, and halls.

The Ghai had cut stairs where the veins dipped, and wide hallways where the veins widened, and here and there his light brushed the ruins of their life, a rusted sled of a design he had never seen, a stack of clay lamps furred with mineral bloom, a wall of tally marks in ordered columns, thousands of them, some accounting kept by hands four hundred years dead.

The sound of the machines came and went with the turnings, closer and farther and closer and Burgundy contemplated what could happen if he got lost down here. But still he followed the sound, and soon he heard a low irregular murmur, almost like water, almost like…
Voices.
He came around a final turn and the tunnel opened, and he stopped at the edge of a space so large his lantern could not propose a shape for it.
His eyes adjusted, and the dark assembled into a cavern the size of the palace Kings' Hall three times over. But this wasn't Ghai ruin.

He saw newer timber shoring, rail lines, ore carts,, a cage elevator hanging in a shaft of work-light that fell from somewhere far above. Broken tools against the walls. Coils of cable. The living infrastructure of a working mine, grafted onto the bones of the dead kingdom.
He knew where he was. He had been here, near here, once, at twelve years old, standing at a rim far above in an embroidered coat.
South 12 Shaft.
And there, across the cavern floor, in the pooled glow of the work-lights, were his machines.
The three DREKKOs had arranged themselves against a broad dark face of corvite, a monster vein, the kind the southern crews called a widow-maker, and they were working it. Calmly. Perfectly.

The nearest one placed a micro-charge with a motion as small as a nod; the crack of it was polite, almost apologetic; a sheet of ore sagged free and the second machine, blinking one red in between two green to indicate it was out of explosives, had given itself the duty of receiving the falling load its partner just cut free of the face. It was crushing, grading, pressing.

Their green panels pulsed in the dark like three calm hearts. They had come out of the palace's foundations, through a dead kingdom, into a live mine, and finding rock, finding ore, finding the thing they had taught themselves to want, they had simply gone back to work.
And in a rough half-circle around them, at the respectful, ready distance stood the miners.
Fifteen of them, maybe more at the edges of the light. Night shift, southern crew, soot-dark faces, picks still in their hands, one man holding a pry bar across his chest like a rifle at parade.

Nobody was working. Nobody was speaking anymore; whatever murmur he had heard had died when the lamplight came around the turning. They had been watching the machines. He could read it in their bodies, the awe and the fear locked together, men watching a shift's tonnage come off a widow-maker vein in perfect silence. And now, one by one, they turned, and they were watching him.
